A(m,m)\cos(\kappa.x+\chi)\right)-\epsilon\mathchoice{A^{{{i}{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{i}{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{i}{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{i}{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{m^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{j}}}}{m^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{j}}}}{m^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{j}}}}{m^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{j}}}}\cos(\kappa.x+\chi)\,.

(6.1.7)

Analogously to the discussion of Maxwell fields in
Section

2
, our boundary conditions (
6.1.1
) fit well into both the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem, which provides a solution in our setting, and the Holmgren uniqueness theorem, which asserts that solutions of such boundary value problems are unique within the class of smooth solutions.
In any case this provides a toy model for the problem at hand, and we provide the unique solution below up to, experimentally irrelevant, error terms
O(\epsilon^{2})
.

For the perturbative setting, consider first
\epsilon=0
(unperturbed problem) where the solution is evidently given by

\displaystyle\phi^{(0)}

\displaystyle=e^{ik.x}\,,

(6.1.8)

where

\displaystyle\mathchoice{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}

\displaystyle=\omega(-1,nm)\,.

(6.1.9)

In the perturbed case, we thus write

\phi=\phi^{(0)}+\epsilon\phi^{(1)}+O(\epsilon^{2})\,.

(6.1.10)

Inserting this into the scalar wave equation (
6.1
) and the boundary conditions (
6.1.1
) leads, at first order in
\epsilon
, to the boundary value problem

\displaystyle\wop_{\gamma^{(0)}}\phi^{(1)}

\displaystyle=-n^{2}\omega^{2}A(m,m)\cos(\kappa.x+\chi)e^{ik.x}\,,

(6.1.11)

\displaystyle\phi^{(1)}|_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle m(\phi^{(1)})|_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle=\tfrac{i}{2}n\omega A(m,m)\cos(\kappa.x+\chi)e^{-i\omega t}\,.

Of course, the right-hand sides are also evaluated at
\Sigma
whenever the left-hand sides are.

6.1.1
General Expression for Emitted Waves

Since we will later consider light emission modelled by Maxwell fields, we will now solve a slightly more general problem (suppressing the superscript “
{(1)}
” momentarily):

\displaystyle\wop_{\gamma^{(0)}}\phi

\displaystyle=-\omega^{2}f_{1}e^{ik.x}\,,

(6.1.12)

\displaystyle\phi|_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle=f_{2}e^{-i\omega t}\,,

(6.1.13)

\displaystyle m(\phi)|_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle=in\omega f_{3}e^{-i\omega t}\,,

(6.1.14)

where
f_{1}
is a trigonometric function (by which we mean a linear combination of
\sin
and
\cos
) of
\kappa.x+\chi
, and
f_{2},f_{3}
are linear combinations of such functions of
\kappa.x|_{\Sigma}+\chi
,
\chi-\omega_{g}t
, and possibly involve additive constants.
This form covers all the boundary values problems, arising in the description of light emission, considered in this work.

We find it useful to expand the trigonometric functions in terms of complex exponentials as follows:

\displaystyle f_{1}

\displaystyle=\alpha^{+}e^{+i(\kappa.x+\chi)}+\alpha^{-}e^{-i(\kappa.x+\chi)}\,,

(6.1.15)

\displaystyle f_{2}

\displaystyle=\beta_{1}^{+}e^{+i(\kappa.x+\chi)}+\beta_{1}^{-}e^{-i(\kappa.x+\chi)}+\gamma_{1}^{+}e^{+i(\chi-\omega_{g}t)}+\gamma_{1}^{-}e^{-i(\chi-\omega_{g}t)}+2\delta_{1}\,,

(6.1.16)

\displaystyle f_{3}

\displaystyle=\beta_{2}^{+}e^{+i(\kappa.x+\chi)}+\beta_{2}^{-}e^{-i(\kappa.x+\chi)}+\gamma_{2}^{+}e^{+i(\chi-\omega_{g}t)}+\gamma_{2}^{-}e^{-i(\chi-\omega_{g}t)}+2\delta_{2}\,,

(6.1.17)

with the right-hand sides of
(
6.1.16
) and (
6.1.17
) implicitly restricted to
\Sigma
.
The factor
2
in front of
\delta_{1}
and
\delta_{2}
is introduced for notational simplicity in the calculations which follow.
The solution to this problem can then be written as

\phi=\phi^{+}+\phi^{-}\,,

(6.1.18)

where
\phi^{+}\equiv\phi^{+}(\alpha^{+},\beta_{1}^{+},\beta_{2}^{+},\gamma_{1}^{+},\gamma_{2}^{+})
is the solution to the problem

\displaystyle\wop_{\gamma^{(0)}}\phi^{+}

\displaystyle=-\alpha^{+}\omega^{2}e^{i(k+\kappa).x+i\chi}\,,

(6.1.19)

\displaystyle\phi^{+}|_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle=(\beta_{1}^{+}e^{i(\kappa.x+\chi)}+\gamma_{1}^{+}e^{i(\chi-\omega_{g}t)}+\delta_{1})e^{-i\omega t}\,,

(6.1.20)

\displaystyle m(\phi^{+})|_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle=in\omega(\beta_{2}e^{i(\kappa.x+\chi)}+\gamma_{2}^{+}e^{i(\chi-\omega_{g}t)}+\delta_{2})e^{-i\omega t}\,,

(6.1.21)

which we will construct shortly, and
\phi^{-}
is obtained from
\phi^{+}
by replacing the various coefficients
\alpha^{+},\beta_{1}^{+},\ldots
by the corresponding quantities
\alpha^{-},\beta_{1}^{-},\ldots
, and reversing the sign of both
\omega_{g}
and
\chi
.

In fact, it is not necessary to write down the phase offset
\chi
explicitly.
Indeed, given a solution for
\chi=0
, the general case is obtained by the substitution

(\alpha^{\pm},\beta_{1,2}^{\pm},\gamma_{1,2}^{\pm})\to e^{\pm i\chi}(\alpha^{\pm},\beta_{1,2}^{\pm},\gamma_{1,2}^{\pm})\,,

(6.1.22)

while keeping
\delta_{1,2}
unchanged.

Hence, we consider the boundary value problem

\displaystyle\wop_{\gamma^{(0)}}\phi

\displaystyle=-\omega^{2}\alpha e^{i(k+\kappa).x}\,,

(6.1.23)

\displaystyle\phi|_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle=(\beta_{1}e^{i\kappa.x}+\gamma_{1}e^{-i\omega_{g}t}+\delta_{1})e^{-i\omega t}\,,

(6.1.24)

\displaystyle m(\phi)|_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle=in\omega(\beta_{2}e^{i\kappa.x}+\gamma_{2}e^{-i\omega_{g}t}+\delta_{2})e^{-i\omega t}\,,

(6.1.25)

for generic parameters
\alpha,\beta_{1,2},\gamma_{1,2},\delta_{1,2}
.
The wave-vectors occurring here are

\displaystyle\mathchoice{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}

\displaystyle=\omega(-1,nm)\,,

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\kappa^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\kappa^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\kappa^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\kappa^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}

\displaystyle=\omega_{g}(-1,{\hat{\kappa}})\,.

(6.1.26)

We constrict explicitly a solution
\phi=\phi(\alpha^{+},\beta^{+},\gamma^{+},\delta)
, which is the unique solution by Holmgren’s theorem.

Construction of the Solution

A particular solution to the inhomogeneous wave equation (
6.1.23
) is

\displaystyle\phi_{\text{part.}}

\displaystyle=-\frac{\alpha}{\Omega\sigma}e^{i(k+\kappa).x}\,,

(6.1.27)

where

\displaystyle\sigma

\displaystyle=-\frac{\mathchoice{\gamma^{{{{(0)}}{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.2611pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\gamma^{{{{(0)}}{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.2611pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\gamma^{{{{(0)}}{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.2611pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\gamma^{{{{(0)}}{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.2611pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{(k+\kappa)^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{(k+\kappa)^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{(k+\kappa)^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{(k+\kappa)^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}\mathchoice{(k+\kappa)^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{(k+\kappa)^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{(k+\kappa)^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{(k+\kappa)^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}}{\omega\omega_{g}}=2n(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})+\Omega(n^{2}-1)\,,

(6.1.28)

provided that
\Omega
and
\sigma
do not vanish. We will assume this in all calculations that follow, and consider the low frequency limit
\Omega\to 0
and the “collinear vacuum limit” (where
n=1
and
m.{\hat{\kappa}}\to 1
so that
\sigma\to 0
) at the end of our calculations.

To satisfy the boundary conditions, we add plane waves which restrict to the desired behaviour on
\Sigma
.
The functions
\exp(i(k+\kappa-\omega\zeta m).x)
and
\exp(i(k-\omega\xi m).x-i\omega_{g}t)
satisfy the homogeneous wave equation for the following values of
\zeta
and
\xi
:

\displaystyle\zeta_{1,2}

\displaystyle=n+\Omega m.{\hat{\kappa}}\mp\sqrt{(n+\Omega m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}+\Omega\sigma}\,,

(6.1.29)

\displaystyle\xi_{1,2}

\displaystyle=n\mp n(1+\Omega)\,,

(6.1.30)

where the first (second) subscript index refers to the upper (lower) sign.
Defining also the reflected wave vector

\mathchoice{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}=\omega(-1,-nm)\,,

(6.1.31)

we make the ansatz

\displaystyle\phi

\displaystyle=\phi_{S}+\phi_{R}\,,

(6.1.32)

with

\displaystyle\phi_{S}

\displaystyle=-\frac{\alpha}{\Omega\sigma}e^{i(k+\kappa).x}\left(1-e^{-i\omega\zeta_{1}m.x}\right)\,,

(6.1.33)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\phi_{R}&=\left(\lambda_{1}e^{-i\omega\zeta_{1}m.x}+\lambda_{2}e^{-i\omega\zeta_{2}m.x}\right)e^{i(k+\kappa).x}\\
&+\left(\mu_{1}e^{-i\omega\xi_{1}m.x}+\mu_{2}e^{-i\omega\xi_{2}m.x}\right)e^{i(k.x-\omega_{g}t)}+\nu_{1}e^{ik.x}+\nu_{2}e^{i\check{k}.x}\,.\end{split}

(6.1.34)

Here we have split the function
\phi
into a “seemingly singular part”
\phi_{S}
which is undefined for
\Omega\sigma=0
, and a remainder
\phi_{R}
. As we will see, both
\phi_{S}
ad
\phi_{R}
have well-behaved low-frequency and collinear vacuum limits.
This ansatz satisfies the boundary conditions (
6.1.24
) and (
6.1.25
) if

\displaystyle\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}

\displaystyle=\beta_{1}\,,

\displaystyle\zeta_{1}\lambda_{1}+\zeta_{2}\lambda_{2}

\displaystyle=\beta_{1}(n+\Omega m.{\hat{\kappa}})-n\beta_{2}-\frac{\alpha\zeta_{1}}{\Omega\sigma}\,,

(6.1.35)

\displaystyle\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}

\displaystyle=\gamma_{1}\,,

\displaystyle\xi_{1}\mu_{1}+\xi_{2}\mu_{2}

\displaystyle=n(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2})\,,

(6.1.36)

\displaystyle\nu_{1}+\nu_{2}

\displaystyle=\delta_{1}\,,

\displaystyle\nu_{1}-\nu_{2}

\displaystyle=\delta_{2}\,,

(6.1.37)

with the solution

\displaystyle\lambda_{1,2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\beta_{1}\pm\frac{n\beta_{2}+\frac{\alpha\zeta_{1}}{\Omega\sigma}}{\sqrt{(n+\Omega m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}+\Omega\sigma}}\right)\,,

(6.1.38)

\displaystyle\mu_{1,2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\gamma_{1}\pm\frac{\gamma_{2}}{1+\Omega}\right)\,,

(6.1.39)

\displaystyle\nu_{1,2}

\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}(\delta_{1}\pm\delta_{2})\,.

(6.1.40)

Recall that for computational reasons
\Omega
is allowed to be negative, but since we are interested in the low-frequency regime
|\Omega|<1
, the case
1+\Omega=0
is irrelevant for our purposes and, in fact, we will assume
1+\Omega>0
.

Emission Condition

Note that
\zeta_{1}
and
\xi_{2}
are of order
\Omega
. The plane waves multiplied by
\lambda_{1}
,
\mu_{1}
and
\nu_{1}
thus have wave vectors which are close to the unperturbed wave vector
k
. In contrast, since
\zeta_{2}
and
\xi_{2}
have an expansion of the form
2n+O(\Omega)
, the plane waves multiplied by
\lambda_{2}
,
\mu_{2}
and
\nu_{2}
correspond to “counter-propagating waves” whose wave vectors are close to the
reflected
wave vector
\check{k}=k-2n\omega m
.

The condition for absence of such counter-propagating components is
\lambda_{2}=\mu_{2}=\nu_{2}=0
, which translates to the following conditions on the boundary data:

\displaystyle\beta_{1}\sqrt{(n+\Omega m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}+\Omega\sigma}-n\beta_{2}-\frac{\alpha\zeta_{1}}{\Omega\sigma}

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle(1+\Omega)\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2}

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle\delta_{1}-\delta_{2}

\displaystyle=0\,.

(6.1.41)

These conditions could have been imposed from the beginning, but the analysis without assuming (
6.1.41
) makes it clear that only a limited subclass of solutions are of the eikonal form.
If these conditions are met, the solution simplifies to

\phi/e^{ik.x}=-\frac{\alpha}{\Omega\sigma}\left(e^{i\kappa.x}-e^{i(\kappa.x-\omega\zeta_{1}m.x)}\right)+\beta_{1}e^{i(\kappa.x-\omega\zeta_{1}m.x)}+\gamma_{1}e^{-i(\omega_{g}t+\omega\xi_{1}m.x)}+\delta_{1}\,.

(6.1.42)

We now consider the following two limiting cases which have been excluded so far:
(i) the collinear vacuum limit where
n=1
and
m.{\hat{\kappa}}\to 1
, so that
\sigma\to 0
according to (
6.1.28
), and (ii) the low frequency limit
\Omega\to 0
.
Both singularities turn out to be removable.

Collinear Vacuum Limit

Consider first the collinear vacuum limit of (
6.1.42
), where
n=1
and
m.{\hat{\kappa}}\to 1
.
The last two terms in (
6.1.42
) remain unchanged in this limit, and the second to last term tends to
\beta_{1}e^{i(\kappa.x)}
since
\zeta_{1}\to 0
in this limit.
Finally, for the remaining term, one has

\lim_{m.{\hat{\kappa}}\to 1}\frac{1}{\Omega\sigma}\left(e^{-i\omega\zeta_{1}m.x}-1\right)=\frac{i\omega m.x}{2(1+\Omega)}\,,

(6.1.43)

so all terms in (
6.1.42
) have a finite collinear vacuum limit.
This shows that the singularity at
m.{\hat{\kappa}}=1
and
n=1
is removable.

Low-Frequency Limit

Next, consider the limit
\Omega\to 0
of (
6.1.42
).
There, one has

\lim_{\Omega\to 0}\frac{1}{\Omega\sigma}\left(e^{-i\omega\zeta_{1}m.x}-1\right)=\frac{i\omega m.x}{2n}\,.

(6.1.44)

Hence, the limit
\Omega\to 0
is also well-behaved and the singularity at
\Omega=0
is removable.

Eikonal Expansion

Using the explicit result (
6.1.42
), one can now prove the claims made in
Section

4
.
The formula just obtained is already reminiscent of (
4.9
), but the exact details require further analysis.

Since
\sigma
is analytic near
\Omega=0
with the expansion
\sigma=2n(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})+O(\Omega)
, one has

\frac{1}{\Omega\sigma}=\frac{1}{2n\Omega(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})}+f(\Omega)\,;

(6.1.45)

here and in what follows
f(\Omega)
denotes a generic function which may change from line to line and which is analytic in
\Omega
in a neighbourhood of zero.
Similarly,
\zeta_{1}
is analytic in
\Omega
in a neighbourhood of zero and has the expansion
\zeta_{1}=\Omega(m.{\hat{\kappa}}-n)+O(\Omega^{2})
. Consequently,
\kappa.x-\omega\zeta_{1}m.x=\kappa_{0}.x+f(\Omega)\omega_{g}m.x
,
where

\kappa_{0}.x:=\kappa.x+(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})\omega_{g}m.x\,.

(6.1.46)

It then follows that

-\frac{\alpha}{\Omega\sigma}\left(e^{i\kappa.x}-e^{i(\kappa.x-\omega\zeta_{1}m.x)}\right)=-\frac{\alpha}{2n\Omega}\frac{e^{i\kappa.x}-e^{i\kappa_{0}.x}}{n-m.{\hat{\kappa}}}+f(\Omega,\kappa.x,\omega_{g}m.x)\,.

(6.1.47)

Similarly, the remaining terms in (
6.1.42
) are of the form
f(\Omega,\kappa.x,\omega_{g}t,\omega_{g}m.x)
: the
\beta_{1}
-term is of the form just considered, and the
\gamma_{1}
-term can be written as
\gamma_{1}e^{i\omega_{g}(t-nm.x)}
.
Putting all this together, one arrives at the result

\phi/e^{ik.x}=-\frac{\alpha}{2n\Omega}\frac{e^{i\kappa.x}-e^{i\kappa_{0}.x}}{n-m.{\hat{\kappa}}}e^{i\kappa.x}+f(\Omega,\kappa.x,\omega_{g}t,\omega_{g}m.x)\,.

(6.1.48)

We are primarily concerned with perturbations of plane waves solutions, with the plane wave taking the form
\phi^{(0)}=\varphi^{(0)}e^{ik.x}
for some constant
\varphi^{(0)}
.
For
\varphi^{(0)}\neq 0
it suffices to consider the case
\varphi^{(0)}=1
by linearity.
In this case, the structure of the wave equation (
4.1
) implies that
\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2}n^{2}A(m,m)+O(\Omega)
so that the overall correction is found to be

\phi^{(1)}=i\psi^{(1)}+f(\Omega,\kappa.x,\omega_{g}t,\omega_{g}m.x)\,,

(6.1.49)

where

\psi^{(1)}=-\tfrac{1}{2}nA(m,m)\frac{\sin(\kappa.x+\chi)-\sin(\kappa_{0}.x+\chi)}{\Omega(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})}\,.

(6.1.50)

By a direct calculation one readily verifies that this function satisfies

\mathchoice{\gamma^{{{{(0)}}{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.2611pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\gamma^{{{{(0)}}{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.2611pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\gamma^{{{{(0)}}{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.2611pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\gamma^{{{{(0)}}{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.2611pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}\mathchoice{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}\psi^{(1)}=\tfrac{1}{2}n^{2}\omega^{2}h(m,m)\,,

(6.1.51)

which is the perturbed eikonal equation (
4.10
).

Alternatively, if the unperturbed field has
\varphi^{(0)}=0
(this occurs, for example, for polarized EM plane waves, where two components of each of the unperturbed electric and magnetic fields are zero),
\alpha
is of order
\Omega
and one obtains instead a formula of the kind
\phi^{(1)}=f(\Omega,\kappa.x,\omega_{g}t,\omega_{g}m.x)
without a leading
1/\Omega
term.

All in all, this proves the claims made in
Section

4
.

Next-To-Leading Order Expansion

For later applications, we give an approximate form of (
6.1.42
) which takes into account both the perturbation of the phase, and also the first correction of the amplitude. Since phase perturbations arise at order
\Omega^{-1}
and the first amplitude corrections arise at order
\Omega^{0}
, the desired approximation is obtained by neglecting terms of order
\Omega
and higher.

At this level of accuracy, the emission conditions (
6.1.41
) simplify to yield

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2n^{2}}+\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}

\displaystyle=O(\Omega)\,,

\displaystyle\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2}

\displaystyle=O(\Omega)\,,

\displaystyle\delta_{1}-\delta_{2}

\displaystyle=O(\Omega)\,.

(6.1.52)

If these conditions are satisfied, the field perturbation is given by (
6.1.42
), in which case one may approximate the phases as

\displaystyle\kappa.x-\omega\zeta_{1}m.x

\displaystyle=\kappa_{0}.x-\frac{1-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{2n}\Omega\omega_{g}m.x+O(\Omega^{2}\omega_{g}m.x)\,,

(6.1.53)

\displaystyle-\omega_{g}t-\omega\xi_{1}m.x

\displaystyle=\Omega k.x\,,

(6.1.54)

where
\kappa_{0}.x
is defined in (
6.1.46
).
Expanding the exponentials in this way and using

\frac{1}{\Omega\sigma}=\frac{1}{2\Omega n(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})}-\frac{n^{2}-1}{4n^{2}(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}+O(\Omega)\,,

(6.1.55)

one arrives at

\begin{split}\phi^{\pm}/e^{ik.x}={}&\mp\alpha^{\pm}\,\frac{e^{\pm i\kappa.x}-e^{\pm i\kappa_{0}.x}}{2\Omega n(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})}+\alpha^{\pm}(n^{2}-1)\frac{e^{\pm i\kappa.x}-e^{\pm i\kappa_{0}.x}}{4n^{2}(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\\
&+\left(\beta_{1}^{\pm}\mp i\alpha^{\pm}\frac{1-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{4n^{2}(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})}\omega_{g}m.x\right)e^{\pm i\kappa_{0}.x}\\
&+\gamma_{1}^{\pm}e^{\pm i\omega_{g}(nm.x-t)}+\delta_{1}+O(\Omega\omega_{g}m.x)+O(\Omega)\,,\end{split}

(6.1.56)

where the first error term grows with the distance
m.x
, but the second is uniform in the distance.

6.1.2
Emitted Scalar Wave

Let us now specialize the general solution just constructed to the concrete problem (
6.1.11
).
Then the coefficients in
(
6.1.15
)—(
6.1.17
) read

\displaystyle\alpha^{\pm}

\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}n^{2}A(m,m)\,,

\displaystyle\beta_{1}^{\pm}

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle\beta_{2}^{\pm}

\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{4}A(m,m)\,,

(6.1.57)

and the other parameters
\gamma_{1,2}^{\pm}
,
\delta_{1,2}
vanish.
These parameters do satisfy the conditions (
6.1.52
), so that one may use (
6.1.56
) to obtain

\begin{split}\phi^{\pm}=-\tfrac{1}{2}A(m,m)e^{ik.x}\bigg[&\pm\frac{n}{2\Omega}\frac{e^{\pm i\kappa.x}-e^{\pm i\kappa_{0}.x}}{n-m.{\hat{\kappa}}}-(n^{2}-1)\frac{e^{\pm i\kappa.x}-e^{\pm i\kappa_{0}.x}}{4(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\\
&\pm i\frac{1-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{4(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})}\omega_{g}m.xe^{\pm i\kappa_{0}.x}\bigg]+O(\Omega\omega_{g}m.x)+O(\Omega)\,,\end{split}

(6.1.58)

Computing
\phi^{(1)}=\phi^{+}+\phi^{-}
and restoring the gravitational wave phase shift
\chi
, the first order perturbation is found to be

\begin{split}\phi^{(1)}=-\tfrac{1}{2}A(m,m)e^{ik.x}\bigg[&\frac{in}{\Omega}\frac{\sin(\kappa.x+\chi)-\sin(\kappa_{0}.x+\chi)}{n-m.{\hat{\kappa}}}\\
&-(n^{2}-1)\frac{\cos(\kappa.x+\chi)-\cos(\kappa_{0}.x+\chi)}{2(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\\
&-\frac{1-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{2(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})}\omega_{g}m.x\sin(\kappa_{0}.x+\chi)\bigg]+O(\Omega\omega_{g}m.x)+O(\Omega)\,.\end{split}

(6.1.59)

Since derivatives of the first term in brackets are of order
\omega
, while those of the remaining terms are of order
\omega_{g}
, we interpret the purely imaginary first term as a phase correction (recall that in geometric optics, the eikonal is assumed to be rapidly varying, while the amplitude is slowly varying), and write the resulting overall field as

\displaystyle\phi

\displaystyle=\mathscr{A}e^{i\psi}+O(\epsilon^{2})+O(\epsilon\Omega)+O(\epsilon\Omega\omega_{g}m.x)\,,

(6.1.60)

where

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathscr{A}&=1+\tfrac{1}{4}\epsilon A(m,m)\bigg[\frac{1-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{n-m.{\hat{\kappa}}}\sin(\kappa_{0}.x+\chi)\omega_{g}m.x\\
&\hskip 85.35826pt+(n^{2}-1)\frac{\cos(\kappa.x+\chi)-\cos(\kappa_{0}.x+\chi)}{(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\bigg]\,,\end{split}

(6.1.61)

\displaystyle\psi

\displaystyle=k.x-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon nA(m,m)\frac{\sin(\kappa.x+\chi)-\sin(\kappa_{0}.x+\chi)}{\Omega(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})}\,.

(6.1.62)

6.2
Reflection At a Mirror

We model the mirror by a timelike hypersurface
\Sigma^{\prime}
with the following reflection properties.
An impinging wave
\phi
gives rise to a reflected wave
\check{\phi}
such that

(a)

the overall field
\phi+\check{\phi}
vanishes on
\Sigma^{\prime}
, and

(b)

the normal derivative of
\check{\phi}
is the same as that of
\phi
.

This is made precise by the equations

\displaystyle(\check{\phi}+\phi)|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle\nu(\check{\phi}-\phi)|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=0\,.

(6.2.1)

To illustrate this in flat space-time, consider a plane wave
\phi=\exp(ik.x)
with
\mathchoice{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}=(-\omega,k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})
impinging on a mirror
\Sigma^{\prime}
, which is described by
x=0
.
Choosing the normal
\nu
to be
\partial/\partial x^{1}
one has
\nu(\phi)|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}=ik_{1}\phi|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}
.
The reflected wave
\check{\phi}=-\exp(i\check{k}.x)
with
\mathchoice{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}=(-\omega,-k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})
then restricts to
-\phi
on
\Sigma^{\prime}
and its normal derivative is

\nu(\check{\phi})|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}=i\mathchoice{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{1}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{1}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{1}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{1}}}}\check{\phi}|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}=-i\mathchoice{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{1}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{1}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{1}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{1}}}}\check{\phi}|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}=i\mathchoice{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{1}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{1}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{1}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{1}}}}\phi|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}=\nu(\phi)|_{\Sigma}\,.

(6.2.2)

Since generic waves can be decomposed into plane waves and this argument applies to every Fourier component individually, these conditions are not restricted to plane waves.

In the case of normal incidence in flat spacetime we have
k_{\mu}=(-\omega,n\omega,0,0)
and
\check{k}_{\mu}=(-\omega,-n\omega,0,0)
. However, we shall work in coordinates which are not necessarily adapted to the reflection surface, with both
\Sigma
and
\Sigma^{\prime}
given by
m.x=\text{const}
.

Here it should be kept in mind that different components of the electromagnetic field behave differently at mirrors. We will use the current model for scalar waves to get a first insight, before considering the full problem using Maxwell’s equations below.

As a simple model for the mirror, we consider the hypersurface

\Sigma^{\prime}=\{\mathchoice{m^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{m^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{m^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{m^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}\mathchoice{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\ell\}\,,

(6.2.3)

where the coefficients
m_{i}
are the same as for the emission surface
\Sigma
.
The emission and reflection surfaces are thus parallel as coordinate-planes and separated by a coordinate distance
\ell
.

6.2.1
General Expression for Reflected Waves

Before computing the reflected field from the incident field (
6.1.60
), we consider a more general problem (much like
Section

6.1.1
) and specialize to the concrete problem later. This will be particularly useful for the discussion of Maxwell fields in
Section

7.5
.

Proceeding as in (
6.1.18
) and following, we thus consider the boundary value problem

\displaystyle\wop_{\gamma^{(0)}}\check{\phi}

\displaystyle=-\check{\alpha}\omega^{2}e^{i(\check{k}+\kappa).x+in\omega\ell}\,,

(6.2.4)

\displaystyle\check{\phi}|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=\left(\check{\beta}_{1}e^{i\kappa.x}+\check{\gamma}_{1}e^{-i\omega_{g}t}+\check{\delta}_{1}\right)e^{-i\omega t}\,,

(6.2.5)

\displaystyle m(\check{\phi})|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=-in\omega\left(\check{\beta}_{2}e^{i\kappa.x}+\check{\gamma}_{2}e^{-i\omega_{g}t}+\check{\delta}_{2}\right)e^{-i\omega t}\,,

(6.2.6)

where the relevant wave vectors are

\displaystyle\mathchoice{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}

\displaystyle=\omega(-1,nm)\,,

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}

\displaystyle=\omega(-1,-nm)\,,

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\kappa^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\kappa^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\kappa^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\kappa^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}

\displaystyle=\omega_{g}(-1,{\hat{\kappa}})\,.

(6.2.7)

Here the phase of the source term in the right-hand side was chosen for convenience (
\check{k}.x+n\omega\ell
restricts to
-\omega t
on
\Sigma^{\prime}
). This is no restriction, as additional phase shifts can always be absorbed in the coefficients
\check{\alpha}
,
\check{\beta}_{1,2}
etc.

As in the previous discussion, we work with a vanishing gravitational phase offset
\chi
.
The general case of non-zero
\chi
is obtained by a substitution similar to (
6.1.22
).

The analysis proceeds in almost the same way as in
Section

6.1.1
.
In fact, the only modification is the sign change of
m
and the addition of phases of the form
e^{in\omega\ell}
. In a way similar to (
6.1.32
), we write

\displaystyle\check{\phi}

\displaystyle=\check{\phi}_{S}+\check{\phi}_{R}\,,

(6.2.8)

where

\displaystyle\check{\phi}_{S}

\displaystyle=-\frac{\check{\alpha}}{\Omega\check{\sigma}}e^{i(\check{k}+\kappa).x+in\omega\ell}\left(1-e^{+i\omega\check{\zeta}_{1}(m.x-\ell)}\right)\,,

(6.2.9)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\check{\phi}_{R}&=\left(\check{\lambda}_{1}e^{i\omega\check{\zeta}_{1}(m.x-\ell)}+\check{\lambda}_{2}e^{i\omega\check{\zeta}_{2}(m.x-\ell)}\right)e^{i(\check{k}+\kappa).x+in\omega\ell}\\
&+\left(\check{\mu}_{1}e^{i\omega\check{\xi}_{1}(m.x-\ell)}+\check{\mu}_{2}e^{i\omega\check{\xi}_{2}(m.x-\ell)}\right)e^{i(\check{k}.x-\omega_{g}t+n\omega\ell)}\\
&+\check{\nu}_{1}e^{i(\check{k}.x+n\omega\ell)}+\check{\nu}_{2}e^{i(k.x-n\omega\ell)}.\end{split}

(6.2.10)

Here the coefficients
\check{\sigma}
,
\check{\zeta}_{1,2}
and
\check{\xi}_{1,2}
are

\displaystyle\check{\sigma}

\displaystyle=2n(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})+\Omega(n^{2}-1)\,,

(6.2.11)

\displaystyle\check{\zeta}_{1,2}

\displaystyle=n-\Omega m.{\hat{\kappa}}\mp\sqrt{(n-\Omega m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}+\Omega\check{\sigma}}\,,

(6.2.12)

\displaystyle\check{\xi}_{1,2}

\displaystyle=n\mp n(1+\Omega)\,,

(6.2.13)

which differ from the previously defined quantities
\sigma
,
\zeta_{1,2}
and
\xi_{1,2}
merely by change of sign of
m
(in particular,
\check{\xi}_{1,2}=\xi_{1,2}
).

To implement the boundary conditions, we now impose

\displaystyle\check{\lambda}_{1}+\check{\lambda}_{2}

\displaystyle=\check{\beta}_{1}\,,

\displaystyle\check{\zeta}_{1}\check{\lambda}_{1}+\check{\zeta}_{2}\check{\lambda}_{2}

\displaystyle=\check{\beta}_{1}(n-\Omega m.{\hat{\kappa}})-n\check{\beta}_{2}-\frac{\check{\alpha}\check{\zeta}_{1}}{\Omega\check{\sigma}}\,,

(6.2.14)

\displaystyle\check{\mu}_{1}+\check{\mu}_{2}

\displaystyle=\check{\gamma}_{1}\,,

\displaystyle\check{\xi}_{1}\check{\mu}_{1}+\check{\xi}_{2}\check{\mu}_{2}

\displaystyle=n(\check{\gamma}_{1}-\check{\gamma}_{2})\,,

(6.2.15)

\displaystyle\check{\nu}_{1}+\check{\nu}_{2}

\displaystyle=\check{\delta}_{1}\,,

\displaystyle\check{\nu}_{2}-\check{\nu}_{2}

\displaystyle=\check{\delta}_{2}\,,

(6.2.16)

with the solution

\displaystyle\check{\lambda}_{1,2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\check{\beta}_{1}\pm\frac{n\check{\beta}_{2}+\frac{\check{\alpha}\check{\zeta}_{1}}{\Omega\check{\sigma}}}{\sqrt{(n-\Omega m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}+\Omega\check{\sigma}}}\right)\,,

(6.2.17)

\displaystyle\check{\mu}_{1,2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\check{\gamma}_{1}\pm\frac{\check{\gamma}_{2}}{1+\Omega}\right)\,,

(6.2.18)

\displaystyle\check{\nu}_{1,2}

\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}(\check{\delta}_{1}\pm\check{\delta}_{2})\,,

(6.2.19)

cf. (
6.1.35
) — (
6.1.40
).

Reflection Condition

As for the emitted wave, we are primarily interested in the case where no counter-propagating terms arise, which means
\check{\lambda}_{2}=\check{\mu}_{2}=\check{\nu}_{2}=0
, or equivalently

\displaystyle\sqrt{(n-\Omega m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}+\Omega\check{\sigma}}\check{\beta}_{1}-n\check{\beta}_{2}-\frac{\check{\alpha}\check{\zeta}_{1}}{\Omega\check{\sigma}}

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle(1+\Omega)\check{\gamma}_{1}-\check{\gamma}_{2}

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle\check{\delta}_{1}-\check{\delta}_{2}

\displaystyle=0\,.

(6.2.20)

If these conditions are met, the field simplifies to

\begin{split}\check{\phi}/e^{i(k.x+n\omega\ell)}={}&-\frac{\check{\alpha}}{\Omega\check{\sigma}}\left(e^{i\kappa.x}-e^{i\kappa.x+i\omega\check{\zeta}_{1}(m.x-\ell)}\right)\\
&+\check{\beta}_{1}e^{i(\kappa.x+\omega\check{\zeta}_{1}(m.x-\ell))}+\check{\gamma}_{1}e^{-i\omega_{g}(t+n(m.x-\ell))}+\check{\delta}_{1}\,.\end{split}

(6.2.21)

Next-To-Leading Order Expansion

Expanding (
6.2.20
) in powers of
\Omega
, and considering that the boundary values for the reflected wave may contain
1/\Omega
terms, the condition for the absence of counter-propagating terms at first order in
\Omega
is found to be

\displaystyle\frac{\check{\alpha}}{2n^{2}}+\check{\beta}_{1}-\check{\beta}_{2}(1-\Omega)

\displaystyle=O(\Omega)\,,

\displaystyle\check{\gamma}_{1}-\check{\gamma}_{2}(1-\Omega)

\displaystyle=O(\Omega)\,,

\displaystyle\check{\delta}_{1}-\check{\delta}_{2}

\displaystyle=O(\Omega)\,.

(6.2.22)

Expanding then the first coefficient in (
6.2.21
) as

\frac{1}{\Omega\check{\sigma}}=\frac{1}{2\Omega n(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})}-\frac{n^{2}-1}{4n^{2}(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}+O(\Omega)\,,

(6.2.23)

cf. (
6.1.55
), and expanding the phase as

\kappa.x+\check{\zeta}_{1}(m.x-\ell)=\kappa_{1}.x-\frac{1-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{2n}\Omega\omega_{g}(\ell-m.x)+O(\Omega^{2}\omega_{g}(\ell-m.x))\,,

(6.2.24)

where

\kappa_{1}.x=\kappa.x+(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})\omega_{g}(\ell-m.x)\,,

(6.2.25)

cf. (
6.1.53
), one arrives at

\begin{split}\check{\phi}^{\pm}/e^{i(\check{k}.x+n\omega\ell)}=&{}\mp\check{\alpha}^{\pm}\frac{e^{\pm i\kappa.x}-e^{\pm i\kappa_{1}.x}}{2\Omega n(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})}+\check{\alpha}^{\pm}(n^{2}-1)\frac{e^{\pm i\kappa.x}-e^{\pm i\kappa_{1}.x}}{4n^{2}(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}+\check{\beta}_{1}^{\pm}e^{\pm i\kappa_{1}.x}\\
&\mp i\frac{1-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{2n}\left[\frac{\check{\alpha}^{\pm}}{2n(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})}\pm\Omega\check{\beta}_{1}^{\pm}\right]\omega_{g}(\ell-m.x)e^{\pm i\kappa_{1}.x}\\
&+\check{\gamma}_{1}^{\pm}e^{\mp i\omega_{g}(t+n(m.x-\ell))}+\check{\delta}_{1}^{\pm}+O(\Omega\omega_{g}(\ell-m.x))+O(\Omega)\,.\end{split}

(6.2.26)

As in (
6.1.56
), the first error term grows with the distance from
\Sigma^{\prime}
, while the second one is uniform in the distance.

6.2.2
Reflected Scalar Wave

In the unperturbed problem
\epsilon=0
, the reflected wave is given by

\displaystyle\check{\phi}^{(0)}

\displaystyle=-e^{i\check{k}.x+2in\omega\ell}\,,

(6.2.27)

where

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\check{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}

\displaystyle=\omega(-1,-nm)\,.

(6.2.28)

In the perturbed case, we thus write

\check{\phi}=\check{\phi}^{(0)}+\epsilon\check{\phi}^{(1)}+O(\epsilon^{2})\,.

(6.2.29)

From the perturbed wave equation (
6.1
) one then finds that
\check{\phi}^{(1)}
satisfies the inhomogeneous wave equation

\wop_{\gamma^{(0)}}\check{\phi}^{(1)}=-n^{2}\omega^{2}A(m,m)\cos(\kappa.x+\chi)\check{\phi}^{(0)}\,,

(6.2.30)

cf. (
6.1.11
).
According to (
6.2.1
), the boundary conditions for
\phi^{(1)}
are

\displaystyle\check{\phi}^{(1)}|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=-\phi^{(1)}|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}\,,

\displaystyle m(\check{\phi}^{(1)})|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=m(\phi^{(1)})|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}+\nu^{(1)}(\phi^{(0)}-\check{\phi}^{(0)})|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}\,.

(6.2.31)

Using the explicit formula (
6.1.7
), one finds that the terms arising from the perturbation of the normal
\nu
cancel, so that it suffices to implement the conditions

\displaystyle\check{\phi}^{(1)}|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=-\phi^{(1)}|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}\,,

\displaystyle m(\check{\phi}^{(1)})|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=m(\phi^{(1)})|_{\Sigma^{\prime}}\,.

(6.2.32)

Using the previously derived expression (
6.1.59
) for the emitted wave and setting

\varpi=(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})\omega_{g}\ell\,

(6.2.33)

such that
\kappa_{0}.x=\kappa.x+\varpi
on
\Sigma^{\prime}
, one finds the coefficients
\check{\alpha}^{\pm}
and
\check{\beta}^{\pm}_{1,2}
in (
6.2.4
) — (
6.2.6
) to be

\displaystyle\check{\alpha}^{\pm}

\displaystyle=-\tfrac{1}{2}n^{2}A(m,m)e^{in\omega\ell\pm i\chi}\,,

(6.2.34)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\check{\beta}_{1}^{\pm}&=\tfrac{1}{4}A(m,m)e^{in\omega\ell\pm i\chi}\bigg[\pm\frac{n}{\Omega}\frac{1-e^{\pm i\varpi}}{n-m.{\hat{\kappa}}}-(n^{2}-1)\frac{1-e^{\pm i\varpi}}{2(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\\
&\hskip 113.81102pt\pm i\omega_{g}\ell\frac{1-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{2(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})}e^{\pm i\varpi}\bigg]+O(\Omega)+O(\Omega\omega_{g}\ell)\,,\end{split}

(6.2.35)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\check{\beta}_{2}^{\pm}&=\check{\beta}_{1}^{\pm}(1\pm\Omega m.{\hat{\kappa}}/n)-\tfrac{1}{4}A(m,m)e^{in\omega\ell\pm i\chi\pm i\varpi}+O(\Omega)+O(\Omega\omega_{g}\ell)\,,\end{split}

(6.2.36)

and the coefficients
\check{\gamma}_{1,2}^{\pm}
,
\check{\delta}_{1,2}
vanish.
These parameters satisfy (
6.2.22
), so that no counter-propagating terms arise (at the considered level of accuracy) and hence (
6.2.26
) applies. This yields the following result for the reflected wave:

\begin{split}\check{\phi}^{\pm}&=\tfrac{1}{4}A(m,m)\check{\phi}^{(0)}e^{\pm i\chi}\bigg[\mp\frac{n}{\Omega}\left(\frac{e^{\pm i\kappa.x}-e^{\pm i\kappa_{1}.x}}{n+m.{\hat{\kappa}}}+\frac{e^{\pm i\kappa_{1}.x}-e^{\pm i\kappa_{1}.x\pm i\varpi}}{n-m.{\hat{\kappa}}}\right)\\
&\pm\frac{i}{2}\frac{1-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{n^{2}-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\left(2m.{\hat{\kappa}}\,\omega_{g}(\ell-m.x)e^{\pm i\kappa_{1}.x}-(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})\omega_{g}(2\ell-m.x)e^{\pm i(\kappa_{1}.x+\varpi)}\right)\\
&+\tfrac{1}{2}(n^{2}-1)\left(\frac{e^{\pm i\kappa.x}-e^{\pm i\kappa_{1}.x}}{(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}+\frac{e^{\pm i\kappa_{1}.x}-e^{\pm i(\kappa_{1}.x+\varpi)}}{(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\right)\bigg]\,.\end{split}

(6.2.37)

Computing the overall field as
\check{\phi}=\check{\phi}^{(0)}+\varepsilon(\check{\phi}^{+}+\check{\phi}^{-})
, we find

\displaystyle\check{\phi}

\displaystyle=-\check{\mathscr{A}}e^{i\check{\psi}}+O(\epsilon^{2})+O(\epsilon\Omega)+O(\epsilon\Omega\omega_{g}\ell)\,,

(6.2.38)

where

\displaystyle\begin{split}\check{\mathscr{A}}&=1-\tfrac{1}{4}\epsilon A(m,m)\bigg[\frac{1-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{n^{2}-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\bigg(2m.{\hat{\kappa}}\,\omega_{g}(\ell-m.x)\sin(\kappa_{1}.x+\chi)\\
&\hskip 99.58464pt-(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})\omega_{g}(2\ell-m.x)\sin(\kappa_{1}.x+\chi+\varpi)\bigg)\\
&\qquad-(n^{2}-1)\bigg(\frac{\cos(\kappa.x+\chi)-\cos(\kappa_{1}.x+\chi)}{(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\\
&\hskip 99.58464pt+\frac{\cos(\kappa_{1}.x+\chi)-\cos(\kappa_{1}.x+\chi+\varpi)}{(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\bigg)\bigg]\,,\end{split}

(6.2.39)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\check{\psi}&=\check{k}.x+2n\omega\ell-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon nA(m,m)\bigg(\frac{\sin(\kappa.x+\chi)-\sin(\kappa_{1}.x+\chi)}{\Omega(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})}\\
&\hskip 99.58464pt+\frac{\sin(\kappa_{1}.x+\chi)-\sin(\kappa_{1}.x+\chi+\varpi)}{\Omega(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})}\bigg)\,.\end{split}

(6.2.40)

To express the returning field in a concise notation and to compare with the final results of Ref.
[
21
]
(see
Section

8
), we define, for any wave-vector
\tilde{k}

H(\tilde{k},u_{2},u_{1})=\frac{\mathchoice{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}\mathchoice{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}}{2\gamma^{(0)}(k,\kappa)}\int_{u_{1}}^{u_{2}}\mathchoice{h^{{{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\ (6.2.41)

so that for the considered metric perturbation
\mathchoice{h^{{{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{h^{{{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{h^{{{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{h^{{{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}(u)=\mathchoice{A^{{{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\t one has

H(k,u_{2},u_{1})=-\tfrac{1}{2}nA(m,m)\frac{\sin u_{2}-\sin u_{1}}{\Omega(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})}\,.

(6.2.42)

The analogous expression with
k
replaced by
\check{k}
is obtained by reversing the sign of
m
.
With this notation, the eikonal perturbation can be written concisely as

\psi^{(1)}=H(\check{k},\kappa.x+\chi,\kappa_{1}.x+\chi)+H(k,\kappa_{1}.x+\chi,\kappa_{1}.x+\chi+\varpi)\,.

(6.2.43)

Similarly, we set

\mathring{H}(\tilde{k},u_{2},u_{1})=\frac{\mathchoice{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\mu}}}}\mathchoice{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}{\tilde{k}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\nu}}}}}{2\gamma^{(0)}(\tilde{k},\kappa)}\left[\mathchoice{h^{{{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][ {h^{{{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{h^{{{\mu}{\nu}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.86232pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.95248pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10892pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.00928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.42052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.72893pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}(u_{1})\right]\,,

(6.2.44)

so that the amplitude perturbation can be written as

\begin{split}{\mathscr{A}}^{(1)}=&-\tfrac{1}{4}A(m,m)\bigg[\frac{1-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{n^{2}-(m.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\bigg(2m.{\hat{\kappa}}\,\omega_{g}(\ell-m.x)\sin(\kappa_{1}.x+\chi)\\
&\hskip 99.58464pt-(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})\omega_{g}(2\ell-m.x)\sin(\kappa_{1}.x+\chi+\varpi)\bigg)\bigg]\\
&+\tfrac{1}{2}(n^{2}-1)\omega_{g}^{2}\left(\frac{\mathring{H}(\check{k},\kappa.x+\chi,\kappa_{1}.x+\chi)}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,\check{k})}+\frac{\mathring{H}(k,\kappa_{1}.x+\chi,\kappa_{1}.x+\chi+\varpi)}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,k)}\right)\,.\end{split}

(6.2.45)

7
Maxwell’s Equations

Consider the source-free Maxwell equations in the form

\displaystyle\mathrm{d}F

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle\divergence{\bar{F}}

\displaystyle=0\,,

(7.1)

where the field strength
F
(a two-form) comprises the electric and magnetic fields
E
and
B
, and the excitation tensor
{\bar{F}}
(a bivector) comprises the fields
D,H
; see (
7.5
) below.
Here “
\mathrm{d}
” denotes the exterior derivative and “
\divergence
” denotes the divergence with respect to the spacetime metric
g
.
In this work, we consider linear isotropic dielectrics only, for which the relationship between
F
and
{\bar{F}}
takes the form

(7.2)

where

]
.

We apply the 3+1 decomposition given in Ref.
[
23
]
, where we use the expansion

\displaystyle j\varepsilon^{ijk}m_{j}\zeta^{*}_{k}

and since the metric perturbation

(7.1.11)

7.2
Boundary Values

In this section, we construct boundary data for Maxwell’s equations on the emission surface
\Sigma=\{m.x=0\}
, which model the radiation sent out by a laser.

Using the expansion (

), the requirement that
Z
be tangent to the emission surface is seen to be equivalent to

on
\Sigma
, so it remains to prescribe the functions
a
and
b
there.

The Unperturbed Case

Before considering the general case, let us briefly return to the unperturbed problem where the spatial metric reduces to the flat Euclidean metric and the surface conormal is given by
\mathchoice{\nu^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\nu^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\nu^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\nu^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}=\mathchoice{m^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{m^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{m^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{m^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}
.

Decomposing the electromagnetic field as in (
7.1.8
) and projecting the field equations (
7.10
) with
\epsilon=0
onto the basis
\zeta,\zeta^{*},m
, one obtains Maxwell’s equations in the form

\displaystyle\zeta(a)+\zeta^{*}(b)+m(c)=0\,,

(7.2.5)

\displaystyle n\partial_{0}a+m(a)-\zeta^{*}(c)=0\,,

(7.2.6)

\displaystyle n\partial_{0}b-m(b)+\zeta(c)=0\,,

(7.2.7)

\displaystyle n\partial_{0}c-\zeta(a)+\zeta^{*}(b)=0\,.

(7.2.8)

The last equation here does not contain any
m
-derivatives and is thus a “constraint equation” for boundary data prescribed on
\Sigma
, while the remaining equations determine the normal derivatives of
a
,
b
and
c
, once their values on
\Sigma
are specified.

In flat space, (
7.2.4
) is equivalent to
b=c=0
on
\Sigma
, so that the “constraint equation” (
7.2.8
) on
\Sigma
reduces to
\zeta(a)=0
. Choosing adapted coordinates
\tilde{x},\tilde{y}
on
\Sigma
such that
\sqrt{2}\zeta=\partial_{\tilde{x}}+j\partial_{\tilde{y}}
(which is always possible by choosing
\partial_{\tilde{x}}
,
\partial_{\tilde{y}}
and
m
to be a right-handed orthonormal basis), this reduces to the Cauchy-Riemann equation

\frac{\partial a}{\partial\tilde{x}}+j\frac{\partial a}{\partial\tilde{y}}=0\,.

(7.2.9)

Requiring
a
to be bounded, one finds that it must be spatially constant (by Liouville’s theorem) and thus a function of time
t
alone.
Hence, one also has
\zeta^{*}(a)=0
, so that (
7.2.5
) yields
m(c)=0
.

Thus, assuming (
7.2.4
) in flat space and requiring the field on
\Sigma
to be bounded, one obtains the following boundary values on the emission surface
\Sigma

\displaystyle n\partial_{0}a+m(a)

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle b=m(b)

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle c=m(c)

\displaystyle=0\,,

(7.2.10)

where
a
is an arbitrary function of time
t
alone.
In particular to describe the emission of monochromatic plane waves of frequency
\omega
, we shall take
a=e^{-i\omega t}
, which entails
m(a)=-in\omega a
.

Note that since all field components satisfy the wave equation,
b
and
c
vanish identically everywhere and
a
is the only remaining degree of freedom.

Let us now consider the perturbed case, where we still consider the fields on
\Sigma
only.
Since
b
and
c

(7.2.11)

Inserting this into the field equations (
7.10
),
one obtains Maxwell’s equations at first order in
\epsilon

\displaystyle\zeta(a^{(1)})+\zeta^{*}(b^{(1)})+m(c^{(1)})

\displaystyle=0\,,

\mathchoice{{\hat{Z}}^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{{\hat{Z}}^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{{\hat{Z}}^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{{\hat{Z}}^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\mathchoice{\zeta^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\zeta^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\zeta^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\zeta^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}(1+j\epsilon\tilde{a})-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon[\mathchoice{\delta^{{{i}{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt] (7.2.20)

where
\tilde{a}
is an arbitrary function.
In components, this is the same as

\displaystyle a

\displaystyle=[1+\epsilon j\tilde{a}-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon h(\zeta^{*},\zeta)]e^{-i\omega t}\,,

\displaystyle b^{(1)}

\displaystyle=-\tfrac{1}{2}h(\zeta,\zeta)e^{-i\omega t}\,,

\displaystyle c^{(1)}

\displaystyle=0\,.

(7.2.21)

Inserting this into (
7.2.15
), the constraint equation reduces to

\zeta(a^{(1)})+a^{(0)}\mathchoice{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.2611pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{i}{j}{k}}}}{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.23616pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.2611pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.47223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{i}{j}{k}}}}{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyl }{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=0\,,

(7.2.22)

which is equivalent to

j\zeta(\tilde{a})+\tfrac{1}{2}\zeta(h(\zeta^{*},\zeta))-\tfrac{1}{2}\zeta^{*}(h(\zeta,\zeta))=0\,.

(7.2.23)

To understand the implications of this equation, suppose we have two solutions
\tilde{a}_{1}
and
\tilde{a}_{2}
.
Then their difference satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equation (
7.2.9
), so that if both functions are bounded, their difference is spatially constant. Hence, the bounded solutions to (
7.2.23
) are parameterised by an arbitrary complex function of time alone.

A simple choice would be to prescribe
\tilde{a}(t,\mathchoice{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=0)=0
.
However, to allow for alternative models of laser emission, which might differ in their prescriptions for the time evolution of the emitted polarisation (e.g. one could demand the polarisation vector to be parallel transported in time in the sense of the perturbed metric), we allow
\tilde{a}
to satisfy

\tilde{a}|_{\mathchoice{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=0}\equiv\alpha(t):=\alpha_{0}+\alpha_{c}\cos(-\omega_{g}t+\chi)+\alpha_{s}\sin(-\omega_{g}t+\chi)\,,

(7.2.24)

where
\alpha_{0}
,
\alpha_{c}
and
\alpha_{s}
(as well as
\chi
) are
j
-real constants.
This means that the emitted polarization vector at the coordinate origin is normalized (corresponding to an energy density at the coordinate origin which remains constant in time), but we allow for perturbations of the plane of polarization which oscillate with the same frequency as the metric perturbation.

As will be shown below, the parameters
\alpha_{0}
,
\alpha_{c}
and
\alpha_{s}
have no impact on the signal detected in the interferometer considered and can thus be set to zero for this concrete application. However, as they describe the perturbation of the emitted polarisation, they would be observable in potential experiments sensitive to light polarisation.
We note also that the precise form of
\alpha(t)
in (
7.2.24
) fits into our calculations without further due, while more general functions would require further analysis.

Defining

\varsigma=\frac{1}{2{\hat{\kappa}}.\zeta}\left[({\hat{\kappa}}.\zeta)A(\zeta^{*},\zeta)-({\hat{\kappa}}.\zeta^{*})A(\zeta,\zeta)\right]\,,

(7.2.25)

the unique solution to the constraint equation (
7.2.23
) which remains bounded on
\Sigma
is found to be

\tilde{a}=j\varsigma[\cos(\kappa.x)-\cos(-\omega_{g}t+\chi)]+\alpha_{0}+\alpha_{c}\cos(-\omega_{g}t+\chi)+\alpha_{s}\sin(-\omega_{g}t+\chi)\,.

(7.2.26)

The first term here has a non-zero
j
-imaginary part and thus describes
\epsilon
-oscillations in the emitted amplitude. Such a behaviour is unavoidable, as it is a consequence of the constraint equation (
7.2.23
).

Having prescribed the field on
\Sigma
, the normal derivatives of
a
,
b^{(1)}
and
c^{(1)}
can now be obtained from the remaining Maxwell equations

\displaystyle (7.2.28)

\displaystyle\zeta(a^{(1)})+\zeta^{*}(b^{(1)})+m(c^{(1)})

\displaystyle=0\,.

(7.2.29)

Similarly to the scalar wave case, from now on we assume
\omega_{g}\ll\omega
.

From (
7.2.27
) it follows that the normal derivative of
a
is

\nu(a)/\omega=ina+O(\Omega)\,,

(7.2.30)

since
n\partial_{0}a=-in\omega a(1+\epsilon O(\omega_{g}/\omega))
by virtue of (
7.2.21
).

Using the explicit form of
b^{(1)}
in (
7.2.21
), we have

\tfrac{1}{\omega}n\partial_{0}b^{(1)}=-inb^{(1)}+O(\omega_{g}/\omega)\,,

(7.2.31)

since
h
varies with frequency
\omega_{g}
only.
Furthermore, since
a^{(0)}
is constant on
\Sigma
but varies rapidly in the direction of
m
(again by a factor
\omega/\omega_{g}
faster than the metric
h
), we have

\begin{split}\tfrac{1}{\omega}j\varepsilon^{ijk}\zeta_{i}\partial_{j}(a^{(0)}\mathchoice{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}})\zeta^{l}&=jm(a^{(0)}/\omega)\varepsilon^{ijk}\zeta_{i}m_{j}\mathchoice{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{ &=-m(a^{(0)}/\omega)h(\zeta,\zeta)+O(\omega_{g}/\omega)\\
&=-ina^{(0)}h(\zeta,\zeta)+O(\omega_{g}/\omega)\\
&=2inb^{(1)}+O(\omega_{g}/\omega)\,,\end{split}

(7.2.32)

where we have used (
7.1.9
),

, and again the explicit form of

given in (

Plugging all this into (

(7.2.33)

Finally, a direct calculation shows that

\zeta^{*}(b^{(1)})=-a^{(0)}\mathchoice{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}}}_{{{i}{j}{k}}}}{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}}}_{{{i}{j}{k}}}}{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}}}_{{{i}{j}{k}}}}{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}}}_{{{i}{j}{k}}}}\zeta^{i}\zeta^{j}\zeta^{*k}\,,
