m(c)=a^{(0)}\left(\mathchoice{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}}}_{{{i}{j}{k}}}}{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}}}_{{{i}{j}{k}}}}{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}}}_{{{i}{j}{k}}}}{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}}}_{{{i}{j}{k}}}}\zeta^{*i}\zeta^{j}\zeta^{k}+\mathchoice{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}}}_{{{i}{j}{k}}}}{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}}}_{{{i}{j}{k}}}}{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}}}_{{{i}{j}{k}}}}{\Gamma^{{{{(1)}}}}_{{{i}{j}{k}}}}\zeta^{i}\zeta^{j}\zeta^{*k}\right)\,.

(7.2.35)

Inserting (

m(c)=\tfrac{1}{2}\omega_{g}a^{(0)}({\hat{\kappa}}.\zeta)A(m,m)\sin(\kappa.x+\chi)\,.

(7.2.36)

To summarize, we have obtained the following boundary data for Maxwell equations on the emission surface
\Sigma=\{m.x=0\}
.

\displaystyle a

\displaystyle=e^{-i\omega t}\left[1+\epsilon j\tilde{a}-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon h(\zeta^{*},\zeta)\right]\,,

(7.2.37)

\displaystyle b^{(1)}

\displaystyle=-\tfrac{1}{2}e^{-i\omega t}h(\zeta,\zeta)\,,

(7.2.38)

\displaystyle c^{(1)}

\displaystyle=0\,,

(7.2.39)

\displaystyle\nu(a)

\displaystyle=in\omega a+O(\omega_{g})\,,

(7.2.40)

\displaystyle\nu^{(0)}(b^{(1)})

\displaystyle=in\omega b^{(1)}+O(\omega_{g})\,,

(7.2.41)

(7.3.5)

{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\zeta^{{{k}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\zeta^{{{k}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=({\hat{\kappa}}.\zeta)A(m,m)\,,

(7.3.13)

which determines
\alpha^{\pm}
to leading order in
\Omega
:

\displaystyle\alpha^{\pm}

\displaystyle=\mp\tfrac{1}{2}n\Omega({\hat{\kappa}}.\zeta)A(m,m)+O(\Omega^{2})\,,

(7.3.14)

while all other parameters vanish to the considered order, as follows from (
7.2.39
) and (
7.2.42
).

Result

All the above parameter sets satisfy the emission condition (
6.1.52
), so that the fields are given by the general formula (
6.1.56
). This yields the following result for the emitted field:

), and where we have used the abbreviations

(7.3.18)

) entails that

so all scalar invariants of the electromagnetic field vanish to the considered accuracy, cf. (

).

7.4
Reflection at a Mirror

Having found the electromagnetic wave emitted from a laser, we now consider its reflection off a perfectly reflecting mirror.

Recall that the jumps (denoted by
\varDelta D,\varDelta B
etc.) of the fields at an interface with unit normal
\nu
satisfy

\displaystyle\nu\cdot\varDelta D

\displaystyle=\mathfrak{s}\,,

\displaystyle\nu\cdot\varDelta B

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle\nu\times\varDelta E

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle\nu\times\varDelta H

\displaystyle=\mathfrak{j}\,,

(7.4.1)

where
\mathfrak{s}
is the surface charge density and
\mathfrak{j}
is the surface current density.

Since all fields vanish inside (or behind) the mirror, the overall field at the reflecting side of the mirror (being a sum of the incident and the reflected fields) satisfies

\displaystyle\nu\cdot D

\displaystyle=\mathfrak{s}\,,

\displaystyle\nu\cdot B

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle\nu\times E

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle\nu\times H

\displaystyle=\mathfrak{j}\,.

(7.4.2)

Let
Z
denote the incident Maxwell field, with
Z^{*}
its
j
-complex conjugate, and let
\check{Z}
be the reflected field.
Using our notation, the standard conditions for reflection on a perfect mirror can be written as

\displaystyle\nu\cdot(\check{Z}-Z^{*})

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle\nu\times(\check{Z}+Z^{*})

\displaystyle=0\,.

(7.4.3)

Indeed, the imaginary part of the first equation is equivalent to
\nu\cdot B=0
, and the real part of the latter is equivalent to
\nu\times E=0
.
The remaining parts (i.e. the real part of the first and the imaginary part of the second equation) say that the surface charges and currents have equal contributions from the incident and the reflected waves, cf. equations (56) and (58) in Ref.
[
24
]
.
This can be understood as follows.
The reflected wave is caused by the movement of charge carriers which respond to the impinging wave as to cancel the field inside the conductor.
But the true sources must be computed from the total field (the incident
and
the reflected wave) and a linear response of the mirror demands that the contributions of both parts are proportional to each other.
Equality then follows from the condition that the amplitudes of the incident and reflected waves coincide.

Equivalently, the equation can be interpreted to say that the normal part of the electric field and the tangential parts of the magnetic field are unchanged by the reflection process, while the tangential part of the electric field and the normal part of the magnetic field change sign.

A covariant formulation of (
7.4.3
) is given in
Appendix

E
.
There, it is also shown that this condition is consistent in the sense that if the incident field
Z
satisfies the constraint equation arising from Maxwell’s equations, then so does the reflected field
\check{Z}
.

The unique solution to (
7.4.3
) is given by

\check{Z}=-Z^{*}+2\mathrm{g}(\nu,Z^{*})\nu\,,

(7.4.4)

i.e.
\check{Z}
is obtained by reflecting
Z
along the normal
\nu
, taking the
j
-complex conjugate and reversing the sign of the field. In other words, equation (
7.4.3
) is equivalent to (
7.4.4
).

Inserting the incident field of the form

Z=a\zeta+\epsilon(b^{(1)}\zeta^{*}+c^{(1)}m)\,,

(7.4.5)

a direct calculation shows that the reflected field is given by

\check{Z}=-a^{*}\zeta^{*}-\epsilon(b^{{(1)}*}\zeta-c^{{(1)}*}m)\,.

(7.4.6)

Writing (everywhere) the field as

\check{Z}=\check{b}\zeta^{*}+\epsilon(\check{a}^{(1)}\zeta+\check{c}^{(1)}m)\equiv(\check{b}^{(0)}+\epsilon\check{b}^{(1)})\zeta^{*}+\epsilon(\check{a}^{(1)}\zeta+\check{c}^{(1)}m)\,,

(7.4.7)

the components of the reflected field on the mirror surface are seen to be

\displaystyle\check{a}^{(1)}

\displaystyle=-b^{(1)}{}^{*}\,,

\displaystyle\check{b}

\displaystyle=-a^{*}\,,

\displaystyle\check{c}^{(1)}

\displaystyle=c^{(1)}{}^{*}\,.

(7.4.8)

Note that by virtue of equation (
7.3.16
), we have

\check{a}^{(1)}=-\tfrac{1}{2}\check{b}^{(0)}h(\zeta^{*},\zeta^{*})\,.

(7.4.9)

Having found the values of the functions
\check{a},\check{b}
and
\check{c}
on the mirror surface
\Sigma^{\prime}
, we must compute their normal derivatives from Maxwell’s equations.
One of the conditions stems from the divergence equation

\nabla_{i}\check{Z}^{i}=0\,,

(7.4.10)

and the other ones are obtained from the evolution equation

n\partial_{0}\check{Z}^{i}+j\varepsilon^{ijk}\mathrm{g}_{kl}\partial_{j}\check{Z}^{l}+j\varepsilon^{ijk}(\partial_{j}\mathrm{g}_{kl})\check{Z}^{l}=0\,.

(7.4.11)

We obtain, using the vector
\theta
defined in (
7.2.17
):

\displaystyle n\partial_{0}\check{b}-\mathchoice{\mathrm{g}^{{{i}{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\mathrm{g}^{{{i}{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\mathrm{g}^{{{i}{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\mathrm{g}^{{{i}{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\theta^{*}_{i}\partial_{j}\check{b}+\epsilon\zeta(\check{c}^{(1)})+j\epsilon\check{b}^{(0)}\varepsilon^{ijk}\zeta_{i}(\partial_{j}\mathchoice{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$} (7.4.12)

\displaystyle n\partial_{0}\check{a}^{(1)}+m(\check{a}^{(1)})-\zeta^{*}(\check{c}^{(1)})+j\varepsilon^{ijk}\zeta_{i}^{*}\partial_{j}(\check{b}^{(0)}\mathchoice{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}})\zeta^{*l}=0\,,

(7.4.13)

\displaystyle n\partial_{0}\check{c}^{(1)}-\zeta(\check{a}^{(1)})+\zeta^{*}(\check{b}^{(1)})+j\varepsilon^{ijk}m_{i}\partial_{j}(\check{b}^{(0)}\mathchoice{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}})\zeta^{*l}=0\,,

(7.4.14)

\displaystyle\zeta(\check{a}^{(1)})+\zeta^{*}(\check{b}^{(1)})+m(\check{c}^{(1)})=0\,.

(7.4.15)

Here we have used the fact that
\check{b}^{(0)}
coincides with the unperturbed reflected scalar wave, defined in (
6.2.27
):

\check{b}^{(0)}\equiv\check{\phi}^{(0)}=-e^{i(\check{k}.x+2n\omega\ell)}\,,

(7.4.16)

and thus
\zeta^{*}(\check{b}^{(0)})=0
.

Equation (
7.4.14
), obtained by contracting the evolution equation with
m_{i}
, is the “constraint equation” which, as shown in
Appendix

E
, is automatically satisfied.

Using the explicit expression for
\theta
from equation (
7.2.19
), we have

\theta^{*}=\nu+\epsilon h(m,\zeta)\zeta^{*}\,,

(7.4.17)

where the second term, proportional to
\zeta^{*}
, gives no contribution in the expression
\mathchoice{\mathrm{g}^{{{i}{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\mathrm{g}^{{{i}{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\mathrm{g}^{{{i}{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\mathrm{g}^{{{i}{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\theta^{*}_{i}\partial_{j}\check{b}
because of
\zeta^{*}(\check{b}^{(0)})=0
, as just shown.
The relevant equations to determine the normal derivatives of the fields are thus

\displaystyle n\partial_{0}\check{b}-\nu(\check{b})+\epsilon\zeta(\check{c}^{(1)})+\epsilon\check{b}^{(0)}j\varepsilon^{ijk}\zeta_{i}(\partial_{j}\mathchoice{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}})\zeta^{*l}=0\,,

(7.4.18)

\displaystyle n\partial_{0}\check{a}^{(1)}+m(\check{a}^{(1)})-\zeta^{*}(\check{c}^{(1)})+j\varepsilon^{ijk}\zeta_{i}^{*}\partial_{j}(\check{b}^{(0)}\mathchoice{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}}{h^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.56946pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.55847pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.11319pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}{l}}}})\zeta^{*l}=0\,,

(7.4.19)

\displaystyle\zeta(\check{a}^{(1)})+\zeta^{*}(\check{b}^{(1)})+m(\check{c}^{(1)})=0\,.

(7.4.20)

From this, it follows that on the mirror surface
\Sigma^{\prime}
it holds that

\displaystyle\nu(\check{b})

\displaystyle=n\mathchoice{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{0}}}}{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{0}}}}{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{0}}}}{\partial^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{0}}}}\check{b}+O(\Omega)\,,

(7.4.21)

\displaystyle m(\check{a}^{(1)})

\displaystyle=-in\omega\check{a}^{(1)}+O(\Omega)\,,

(7.4.22)

\displaystyle m(\check{c}^{(1)})

\displaystyle=-in\omega\check{c}^{(1)}+O(\Omega)\,.

(7.4.23)

The first equation is immediate, since tangential derivatives of
\check{c}^{(1)}
and all derivatives of the perturbed metric are of order

, as can be seen from (

) and (

).

but must analyse the last term, where the main contribution comes from the derivative of
\check{b}^{(0)}
in the direction of

:

&=h(\zeta^{*},\zeta^{*})m(\check{b}^{(0)})/\omega+O(\Omega)\\
&=-inh(\zeta,\zeta)^{*}\check{b}^{(0)}+O(\Omega)\\
&=2in\check{a}^{(1)}+O(\Omega),\end{split}

(7.4.24)

where we have used (
7.1.9
),
m(\check{b}^{(0)})=-in\omega\check{b}
, which is the unperturbed form of (
7.4.21
), and (
7.4.9
).
Finally, to arrive at the last equation, one can use (
7.4.8
) obtain

m(\check{c}^{(1)})=\zeta^{*}(a^{{(1)}*})+\zeta(b^{{(1)}*})\,.

(7.4.25)

Using the fact that the incident field satisfies

\zeta(a^{(1)})+\zeta^{*}(b^{(1)})+m(c^{(1)})=0\,,

(7.4.26)

as well as the explicit form of
c^{(1)}
in (
7.3.17
), and also the reflection condition (
7.4.8
), one obtains

m(\check{c}^{(1)})/\omega=-m(c^{(1)})^{*}/\omega=-inc^{(1)}+O(\Omega)=-in\check{c}^{(1)}+O(\Omega)\,,

(7.4.27)

which establishes (
7.4.23
).

7.5
The Reflected Wave

The unperturbed reflected wave is evidently given by

(7.5.5)

The components
\check{a}^{(1)}
,
\check{b}^{(1)}
and
\check{c}^{(1)}
can now be determined using the general formulae of
Section

6.2.1
. As done there, we momentarily suppress the GW phase offset
\chi
for notational simplicity and reinstate it only in the final result of the computed field.

The
\check{a}
Component

For the component
\check{a}^{(1)}
, the value of
\check{\alpha}^{\pm}
can be read from (
7.5.3
), and
\check{\beta}^{\pm}_{1}
is determined by
-(b^{(1)})^{*}
according to (
7.4.8
), which is given explicitly in (
7.3.16
). Similarly,
\check{\beta}^{\pm}_{2}
is determined from (
7.4.22
). The such obtained non-vanishing parameters are

\displaystyle\check{\alpha}^{\pm}/e^{in\omega\ell}

\displaystyle=\mp\tfrac{1}{2}n\Omega(n+m.{\hat{\kappa}})A(\zeta^{*},\zeta^{*})+O(\Omega^{2})\,,

(7.5.6)

\displaystyle\check{\beta}^{\pm}_{1,2}/e^{in\omega\ell}

\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{4}A(\zeta^{*},\zeta^{*})+O(\Omega)+O(\Omega\omega_{g}\ell)\,.

(7.5.7)

The
\check{b}
Component

For the component
\check{b}^{(1)}
, the parameter
\check{\alpha}^{\pm}
is determined from (
7.5.4
),
\check{\beta}^{\pm}_{1}
is determined from
-(a^{(1)})^{*}
according to (
7.4.8
), which is given explicitly in (
7.3.15
), and
\check{\beta}^{\pm}_{2}
can be obtained from (
7.4.21
).
These coefficients almost coincide with those for the reflected scalar wave given in (
6.2.34
)-(
6.2.36
).

(7.5.9)

\displaystyle\check{\gamma}^{\pm}_{1,2}/e^{in\omega l}

(7.5.11)

The
\check{c}
Component

For the last component,
\check{c}^{(1)}
, the parameter
\check{\alpha}^{\pm}
can be inferred from (
7.5.5
),
\check{\beta}^{\pm}_{1}
is determined from the incident field
c^{(1)}
in accordance with (
7.4.8
), which is given explicitly in (
7.3.17
), and the parameter
\check{\beta}^{\pm}_{2}
is determined from (
7.4.23
).
To the considered level of approximation, the non-vanishing parameters are thus found to be

\displaystyle\check{\alpha}^{\pm}/e^{in\omega\ell}

\displaystyle=\mp\tfrac{1}{2}n\Omega({\hat{\kappa}}.\zeta^{*})A(m,m)+O(\Omega^{2})\,,

(7.5.12)

\displaystyle\check{\beta}^{\pm}_{1,2}/e^{in\omega\ell}

\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{4}({\hat{\kappa}}.\zeta^{*})A(m,m)\frac{1-e^{\pm i\varpi}}{n-m.{\hat{\kappa}}}+O(\Omega)+O(\Omega\omega_{g}\ell)\,,

(7.5.13)

where
\varpi
is defined in (
6.2.33
).

8
Michelson Interferometers

We are now in a position to describe the gravitational wave response of a Michelson interferometer, as sketched in
Figure

1
.

Figure 1
:
Schematic drawing of a Michelson interferometer.

We use the approach of Ref.
[
21
]
to describe such interferometers.
In Minkowski spacetime, i.e. the unperturbed geometry, let
m_{\textsc{i}}
and
m_{\textsc{ii}}
denote the unit vectors pointing along the two interferometer arms (away from the beam splitter), defining the two emission surfaces
\Sigma_{\textsc{i}}=\{m_{\textsc{i}}.x=0\}
and
\Sigma_{\textsc{ii}}=\{m_{\textsc{ii}}.x=0\}
.
The laser emits coherent light with wave vector
k=\omega(m_{\textsc{i}}-\mathrm{d}t)
and polarisation
\zeta
.
Part of the ray passes through the beam splitter unchanged except for a reduction in amplitude, and thus defines boundary data on
\Sigma_{\textsc{i}}
, corresponding to normal emission with frequency
\omega
and polarisation
\zeta
.
Similarly, the deflected part of the beam gives rise to boundary data on
\Sigma_{\textsc{ii}}
, corresponding again to normal emission with frequency
\omega
, but with the polarisation vector
\eta=R_{\text{BS}}^{(0)}\zeta
where
R_{\text{BS}}^{(0)}
is the orthogonal matrix interchanging
m_{\textsc{i}}
and
m_{\textsc{ii}}
while leaving their orthogonal complements unchanged (see below for details).
There is also a phase shift at the beam splitter, which depends upon the details of the apparatus
[
25
, Section 2.4]
. Since overall phases are irrelevant for our analysis, it suffices to include the relative phase shift of
\pi
in the Michelson interferometer, which we incorporate in the output field below; see (
8.3
).

This description of the beam splitter can be carried over to the perturbed geometry with minimal modifications.
To this end, we prescribe boundary data for Maxwell’s equations on the same surfaces
\Sigma_{\textsc{i}}
and
\Sigma_{\textsc{ii}}
(whose unit normal one-forms
\nu_{\textsc{i}}
and
\nu_{\textsc{ii}}
are proportional to
m_{\textsc{i}}
and
m_{\textsc{ii}}
, respectively) as in the Minkowski case.
We assume again normal emission from both surfaces
\Sigma_{\textsc{i}}
and
\Sigma_{\textsc{ii}}
, and the polarisation on
\Sigma_{\textsc{i}}
is assumed to be of the form given in (
7.2.20
) (as dictated by the assumption of normal emission of plane waves), with the polarisation on
\Sigma_{\textsc{ii}}
(sent into the second arm) related to the one on
\Sigma_{\textsc{i}}
by the orthogonal map
R_{\text{BS}}
which now interchanges
\nu_{\textsc{i}}
and
\nu_{\textsc{ii}}
while leaving their orthogonal complement untouched.

A simple renaming of the relevant data in the solutions derived above provides then the new solutions, as needed to determine the resulting field at the interferometer output.

As such, there are various readout schemes used in gravitational wave detection. For simplicity, we focus here on the DC readout scheme currently used in the LIGO and Virgo detectors. In this scheme, the arm lengths are chosen to be unequal (
\Delta\ell=\ell_{\textsc{i}}-\ell_{\textsc{ii}}\neq 0
) such that even in the absence of a gravitational wave there is a constant output signal registered by the
photodiode, and the gravitational wave then causes a small fluctuation of this signal, which we determine below.

To describe the output of the interferometer, we collect the results obtained so far to describe the field returning to the beam splitter as a function of the emitted field.
We then use our model of the beam splitter to describe how the output of the laser is transferred into the two interferometer arms,
and to describe how the returning rays are transferred to the detector.

The Returning Field

n^{2}\omega_{g}\omega\Delta h\bigg]\\
&\quad-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon\zeta\,h(\zeta^{*},\zeta^{*})+\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon m\,n\omega_{g}\omega(\zeta^{*}.{\hat{\kappa}})\Delta h\,.\end{split}

(8.1.14)

Since the returning field at the origin only involves the function
\tilde{a}
evaluated again at the spatial coordinate origin (but at a retarded time) the
\varsigma
terms in (
8.1.5
), which were necessary to satisfy the constraint equations, are irrelevant for the interferometer output.

This expression serves as the basis for the description of interferometers, as it describes how light emitted from a surface
\Sigma
returns after being reflected at a perfect mirror placed a distance
\ell
away.

8.2
Non-Polarising Beam Splitters

To relate the light polarisation vectors sent into the two interferometer arms (which are both derived from the incoming laser beam) and to compute the output laser field from the returning light rays, one must model the polarisation transfer at the beam splitter.
Following the model put forward in
[
21
]
, we assume the polarisation of the field emitted by the laser to have the form

{\hat{Z}}_{\text{in}}|_{\mathchoice{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=0}=\sqrt{2}\zeta(1+\epsilon j\alpha-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon h(\zeta^{*},\zeta))-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon h(\zeta,\zeta)\zeta^{*}\,,

(8.2.1)

as already considered in the previous calculation (up to the scaling factor
\sqrt{2}
which is conventional).
Assuming a 50:50 beam splitter, the amplitudes of the two rays transferred to the two arms are reduced by a factor
1/\sqrt{2}
. Concerning the polarisation vectors, we assume that the part of the ray which passes straight through the beam splitter maintains its polarisation, while the polarisation sent into the orthogonal arm is given by applying the transformation

\displaystyle{\hat{Z}}\mapsto-R_{\textsc{bs}}{\hat{Z}}^{*}\,,

(8.2.2)

analogously to
eq.

7.4.4
, where
R_{\textsc{bs}}
is the orthogonal matrix
which interchanges the unit conormals
\nu_{\textsc{i}}\propto m_{\textsc{i}}
and
\nu_{\textsc{ii}}\propto m_{\textsc{ii}}
(see
Figure

1
)

\mathchoice{{R_{\textsc{bs}}}^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}{{R_{\textsc{bs}}}^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}{{R_{\textsc{bs}}}^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}{{R_{\textsc{bs}}}^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}=\mathchoice{\delta^{{{i}}}_{{{j}}}}{\delta^{{{i}}}_{{{j}}}}{\delta^{{{i}}}_{{{j}}}}{\delta^{{{i}}}_{{{j}}}}-[1-g(\nu_{\textsc{i}},\nu_{\textsc{ii}})]^{-1}\mathchoice{g^{{{i}{k}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{g^{{{i}{k}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{g^{{{i}{k}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{g^{{{i}{k}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{(\nu_{\textsc{ii}}-\nu_{\textsc{i}})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}}}}{(\nu_{\textsc{ii}}-\nu_{\textsc{i}})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}}}}{(\nu_{\textsc{ii}}-\nu_{\textsc{i}})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}}}}{(\nu_{\textsc{ii}}-\nu_{\textsc{i}})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{k}}}}\mathchoice{(\nu_{\textsc{ii}}-\nu_{\textsc{i}})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{j}}}}{(\nu_{\textsc{ii}}-\nu_{\textsc{i}})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{j}}}}{(\nu_{\textsc{ii}}-\nu_{\textsc{i}})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{j}}}}{(\nu_{\textsc{ii}}-\nu_{\textsc{i}})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{j}}}}\,.

(8.2.3)

As shown in
Appendix

F
, see (
F.24
), the action of this operator on the polarisation vector (
7.2.20
) yields

\begin{split}R_{\textsc{bs}}[&\zeta(1+\epsilon j\alpha-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon h(\zeta^{*},\zeta))-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon\zeta^{*}\,h(\zeta,\zeta)]\\
&=\eta(1+\epsilon j(\alpha+\breve{a})-\tfrac{1}{2}h(\eta^{*},\eta^{*}))-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon\eta^{*}\,h(\eta,\eta)\,,\end{split}

(8.2.4)

where
\eta
is the unperturbed polarisation vector of the second arm:

\eta=\zeta-(m_{\textsc{ii}}-m_{\textsc{i}})(m_{\textsc{ii}}.\zeta)\,,

(8.2.5)

and
\breve{a}
is the
j
-imaginary part of the function
h(\zeta^{*},\zeta-\eta)
:

\breve{a}=\Im_{j}[h(\zeta^{*},\zeta-\eta)]\,.

(8.2.6)

For the returning rays, the behaviour of the fields is similar. The ray which first passed through the beam splitter without deflection is now deflected towards the detector and thus undergoes the transformation (
8.2.2
) with its amplitude reduced by
1/\sqrt{2}
.
The other beam, which was deflected before completing its round trip, now maintains its polarisation vector when being transferred towards the detector. Similarly to the first ray, its amplitude is reduced by
1/\sqrt{2}
, but additionally there is the standard phase shift of
\pi
.

For a more detailed description of the beam splitter transformations, see
[
21
, Sect. 6]
.

8.3
Output Field

We are now in the position to compute the output field reaching the detector, which is a sum of the fields from the two interferometer arms.

Ray I

Consider the ray which is deflected only after its round-trip in one of the interferometer arms.
According to our model of the beam splitter, the corresponding field emanating from
\Sigma_{\textsc{i}}
is thus (see (
8.1.4
)—(
8.1.5
))

Z_{{\textsc{i}}\,\text{in}}|_{\mathchoice{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=0}=+e^{-i\omega t}[\zeta(1+\epsilon\alpha-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon h(\zeta^{*},\zeta))-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon\zeta^{*}\,h(\zeta,\zeta)]\,.

(8.3.1)

The returning field is given by (
8.1.11
)—(
8.1.14
).
To evaluate this at the coordinate origin, we set

\displaystyle u^{E}_{{\textsc{i}}}

\displaystyle=u+2n\omega_{g}\ell_{{\textsc{i}}}\,,

\displaystyle u^{R}_{{\textsc{i}}}=u+(n+{\hat{\kappa}}.m_{\textsc{i}})\omega_{g}\ell_{{\textsc{i}}}\,.

(8.3.2)

Recall that at the coordinate origin we have
u|_{\mathchoice{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=0}=-\omega_{g}t+\chi
.
Applying the beam splitter transformation (
8.2.2
), reducing the amplitude by
1/\sqrt{2}
, and taking the
i
-real part, one obtains the contribution of this ray to the field at the detector output

\displaystyle Z_{\textsc{i}}

\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{\mathscr{A}}_{\textsc{i}}{\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{i}}\cos(\psi_{\textsc{i}})\,,

(8.3.3)

where

\displaystyle\psi_{\textsc{i}}

\displaystyle=-\omega t+2n\omega\ell_{\textsc{i}}+\epsilon H(\check{k}_{\textsc{i}},u,u^{R}_{\textsc{i}})+\epsilon H(k_{\textsc{i}},u^{R}_{\textsc{i}},u^{E}_{\textsc{i}})\,,

(8.3.4)

\displaystyle\begin{split}{\mathscr{A}}_{\textsc{i}}&=1-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon\omega_{g}\ell_{\textsc{i}}A(m_{\textsc{i}},m_{\textsc{i}})\frac{1-(m_{\textsc{i}}.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{n^{2}-(m_{\textsc{i}}.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\left[(m_{\textsc{i}}.{\hat{\kappa}})\sin(u^{R}_{\textsc{i}})-(n+m_{\textsc{i}}.{\hat{\kappa}})\sin(u^{E}_{\textsc{i}})\right]\\
&\qquad+\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon(n^{2}-1)\omega_{g}^{2}\left[\frac{H(\check{k}_{\textsc{i}},u,u^{R}_{\textsc{i}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,\check{k}_{\textsc{i}})}+\frac{H(k_{\textsc{i}},u^{R}_{\textsc{i}},u^{E}_{\textsc{i}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,k_{\textsc{i}})}\right]\,,\end{split}

(8.3.5)

\displaystyle\begin{split}{\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{i}}&=\eta\bigg[1+\epsilon j(\alpha(t-2n\ell_{\textsc{i}})+\breve{a}(t))-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon h(\eta^{*},\eta)+\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon h(\zeta^{*},\zeta)\big|^{u}_{u^{E}_{\textsc{i}}}\\
&\qquad-\epsilon\mathchoice{\zeta^{{{*}}}_{{{i}}}}{\zeta^{{{*}}}_{{{i}}}}{\zeta^{{{*}}}_{{{i}}}}{\zeta^{{{*}}}_{{{i}}}}[\mathchoice{\varGamma^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}{\varGamma^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}{\varGamma^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}{\varGamma^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}(\check{k}_{\textsc{i}},u,u^{R}_{\textsc{i}})+\mathchoice{\varGamma^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.6 criptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}+\tfrac{1}{4}\epsilon n^{2}\omega_{g}\omega\Delta h_{\textsc{i}}\bigg]\\
&\quad-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon\eta^{*}\,h(\eta,\eta)+\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon m_{\textsc{ii}}\,n\omega_{g}\omega({\hat{\kappa}}.\zeta)\Delta h_{\textsc{i}}\,,\end{split}

(8.3.6)

and

\Delta h_{\textsc{i}}:=\frac{h(m_{\textsc{i}},m_{\textsc{i}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,\check{k}_{\textsc{i}})}\bigg|^{u}_{u^{R}_{\textsc{i}}}+\frac{h(m_{\textsc{i}},m_{\textsc{i}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,k_{\textsc{i}})}\bigg|^{u^{R}_{\textsc{i}}}_{u^{E}_{\textsc{i}}}\,.

(8.3.7)

Ray II

The other ray is deflected at the beam splitter before the round-trip.
The corresponding field emanating from
\Sigma_{\textsc{ii}}
is

Z_{{\textsc{ii}}\,\text{in}}|_{\mathchoice{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=0}=-e^{-i\omega t}[\eta^{*}(1-\epsilon j(\alpha+\breve{a})-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon h(\eta^{*},\eta))-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon\eta\,h(\eta^{*},\eta^{*})]\,,

(8.3.8)

and the returning field is directly obtained from (
8.1.11
)—(
8.1.14
) via the substitutions

\displaystyle\zeta

\displaystyle\to\eta^{*}\,,

\displaystyle\zeta^{*}

\displaystyle\to\eta\,,

\displaystyle\alpha

\displaystyle\to-(\alpha+\breve{a})

\displaystyle m

\displaystyle\to m_{\textsc{ii}}

\displaystyle k

\displaystyle\to k_{\textsc{ii}}\,,

(8.3.9)

together with a change of the overall sign. This ray passes through the beam splitter with its amplitude reduced by
1/\sqrt{2}
and the phase shifted by
\pi
, but without modification of the polarisation vector.
Finally, taking the
i
-real part to obtain the physical field, the contribution to the output field from this ray is

\displaystyle Z_{\textsc{ii}}

\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{\mathscr{A}}_{\textsc{ii}}{\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{ii}}\cos(\psi_{\textsc{ii}})\,,

(8.3.10)

where

\displaystyle\psi_{\textsc{ii}}

\displaystyle=-\omega t+2n\omega\ell_{\textsc{ii}}+\pi+\epsilon H(\check{k}_{\textsc{ii}},u,u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}})+\epsilon H(k_{\textsc{ii}},u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}},u^{E}_{\textsc{ii}})\,,

(8.3.11)

\displaystyle\begin{split}{\mathscr{A}}_{\textsc{ii}}&=1-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon\omega_{g}\ell_{\textsc{ii}}A(m_{\textsc{ii}},m_{\textsc{ii}})\frac{1-(m_{\textsc{ii}}.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{n^{2}-(m_{\textsc{ii}}.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\left[(m_{\textsc{ii}}.{\hat{\kappa}})\sin(u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}})-(n+m_{\textsc{ii}}.{\hat{\kappa}})\sin(u^{E}_{\textsc{ii}})\right]\\
&\qquad+\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon(n^{2}-1)\omega_{g}^{2}\left[\frac{H(\check{k}_{\textsc{ii}},u,u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,\check{k}_{\textsc{ii}})}+\frac{H(k_{\textsc{ii}},u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}},u^{E}_{\textsc{ii}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,k_{\textsc{ii}})}\right]\,,\end{split}

(8.3.12)

\displaystyle\begin{split}{\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{ii}}&=\eta\bigg[1+\epsilon j(\alpha(t-2n\ell_{\textsc{ii}})+\breve{a}(t-2n\ell_{\textsc{ii}}))-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon h(\eta^{*},\eta)\\
&\qquad-\epsilon\mathchoice{\eta^{{{*}}}_{{{i}}}}{\eta^{{{*}}}_{{{i}}}}{\eta^{{{*}}}_{{{i}}}}{\eta^{{{*}}}_{{{i}}}}[\mathchoice{\varGamma^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}{\varGamma^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}{\varGamma^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}{\varGamma^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}(\check{k}_{\textsc{ii}},u,u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}})+\mathchoice{\varGamma^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}{\varGamma^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}{\varGamma^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}{\varGamma^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}}(k_{\textsc{ii}},u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}},u^{E}_{\textsc{ii}})]\mathchoice{\eta^{{{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\eta^{{{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\eta^{{{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\eta^{{{j}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}+\tfrac{1}{4}\epsilon n^{2}\omega_{g}\omega\Delta h_{\textsc{ii}}\bigg]\\
&\quad-\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon\eta^{*}\,h(\eta,\eta)+\tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon m_{\textsc{ii}}\,n\omega_{g}\omega({\hat{\kappa}}.\eta)\Delta h_{\textsc{ii}}\,,\end{split}

(8.3.13)

with

\Delta h_{\textsc{ii}}:=\frac{h(m_{\textsc{ii}},m_{\textsc{ii}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,\check{k}_{\textsc{ii}})}\bigg|^{u}_{u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}}}+\frac{h(m_{\textsc{ii}},m_{\textsc{ii}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,k_{\textsc{ii}})}\bigg|^{u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}}}_{u^{E}_{\textsc{ii}}}\,,

(8.3.14)

and

\displaystyle u^{E}_{{\textsc{ii}}}

\displaystyle=u+2n\omega_{g}\ell_{{\textsc{ii}}}\,,

\displaystyle u^{R}_{{\textsc{ii}}}=u+(n+{\hat{\kappa}}.m_{\textsc{ii}})\omega_{g}\ell_{{\textsc{ii}}}\,.

(8.3.15)

8.4
Output Power

Adding the results of the two previous sections, the physical field at the output of the interferometer is found to be

Z_{\text{out}}=Z_{\textsc{i}}+Z_{\textsc{ii}}\equiv\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{\mathscr{A}}_{\textsc{i}}{\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{i}}\cos(\psi_{\textsc{i}})+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{\mathscr{A}}_{\textsc{ii}}{\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{ii}}\cos(\psi_{\textsc{ii}})\,,

(8.4.1)

whose energy density is proportional to the norm

\mathchoice{T^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{0}{0}}}}{T^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{0}{0}}}}{T^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{0}{0}}}}{T^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{0}{0}}}}\propto g(Z_{\textsc{i}}^{*}+Z_{\textsc{ii}}^{*},Z_{\textsc{i}}+Z_{\textsc{ii}})\,,

(8.4.2)

compare
Appendix

D
.
The exact proportionality factor is irrelevant for our purposes, as we are concerned only with the ratio of the output power relative to the input power. Following the standard time-averaging procedure, which we denote by
\langle\cdot\rangle
, we find the observable output power, normalised to the input power, to be

P=\langle g(Z_{\text{out}}^{*},Z_{\text{out}})\rangle/\langle g(Z_{\text{in}}^{*},Z_{\text{in}})\rangle\,.

(8.4.3)

As we have normalised the input field (
8.2.1
) to
\langle g(Z_{\text{in}}^{*},Z_{\text{in}})\rangle=1
, we get

\begin{split}P&=\langle g(Z^{*}_{\textsc{i}}+Z^{*}_{\textsc{ii}},Z_{\textsc{i}}+Z_{\textsc{ii}})\rangle\\
&=\tfrac{1}{4}{\mathscr{A}}_{\textsc{i}}^{2}g({\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{i}}^{*},{\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{i}})+\tfrac{1}{4}{\mathscr{A}}_{\textsc{ii}}^{2}g({\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{ii}}^{*},{\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{ii}})+\tfrac{1}{4}{\mathscr{A}}_{\textsc{i}}{\mathscr{A}}_{\textsc{ii}}[g({\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{i}}^{*},{\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{ii}})+g({\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{i}},{\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{ii}}^{*})]\cos(\psi_{\textsc{i}}-\psi_{\textsc{ii}})\,.\end{split}

(8.4.4)

This is directly measured in the commonly used DC readout scheme of gravitational wave detectors.
In the unperturbed case, the normalised output power takes the simple form

P^{(0)}=\tfrac{1}{2}-\tfrac{1}{2}\cos(2n\omega\Delta\ell)=\sin^{2}(n\omega\Delta\ell)\,,

(8.4.5)

which vanishes for
\Delta\ell\equiv\ell_{\textsc{i}}-\ell_{\textsc{ii}}=0
.
In the perturbed case, a direct calculation based on
eqs.

8.3.6
and
8.3.13
shows that

\displaystyle g({\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{i}}^{*},{\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{i}})

\displaystyle=1+\epsilon n^{2}\omega_{g}\omega\Delta h_{\textsc{i}}\,,

(8.4.6)

\displaystyle g({\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{ii}}^{*},{\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{ii}})

\displaystyle=1+\epsilon n^{2}\omega_{g}\omega\Delta h_{\textsc{ii}}\,,

(8.4.7)

\displaystyle 2\Re_{j}g({\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{i}}^{*},{\hat{Z}}_{\textsc{ii}})

\displaystyle=2+\epsilon n^{2}\omega_{g}\omega[\Delta h_{\textsc{i}}+\Delta h_{\textsc{ii}}]\,.

(8.4.8)

Using the explicit form of the phase and amplitude perturbations given by
eqs.

8.3.4
,
8.3.5
,
8.3.11
and
8.3.12
, one finds that the perturbed output power can be written in the form

P=P^{(0)}+\epsilon\delta_{\psi}P+\epsilon\delta_{\mathscr{A}}P+\epsilon\delta_{n}P+\epsilon\delta_{K}P+O(\epsilon^{2})\,,

(8.4.9)

where

\displaystyle\begin{split}\delta_{\psi}P={}&\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(2n\omega\Delta\ell)\\
&\times\left(H(\check{k}_{\textsc{i}},u,u^{R}_{\textsc{i}})+H(k_{\textsc{i}},u^{R}_{\textsc{i}},u^{E}_{\textsc{i}})-H(\check{k}_{\textsc{ii}},u,u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}})-H(k_{\textsc{ii}},u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}},u^{E}_{\textsc{ii}})\right)\,,\end{split}

(8.4.10)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\delta_{\mathscr{A}}P={}&-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin^{2}(n\omega\Delta\ell)\\
&\times\bigg(\omega_{g}\ell_{\textsc{i}}A(m_{\textsc{i}},m_{\textsc{i}})\frac{1-(m_{\textsc{i}}.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{n^{2}-(m_{\textsc{i}}.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\left[(m_{\textsc{i}}.{\hat{\kappa}})\sin(u^{R}_{\textsc{i}})-(n+m_{\textsc{i}}.{\hat{\kappa}})\sin(u^{E}_{\textsc{i}})\right]\\
&\qquad+\omega_{g}\ell_{\textsc{ii}}A(m_{\textsc{ii}},m_{\textsc{ii}})\frac{1-(m_{\textsc{ii}}.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}{n^{2}-(m_{\textsc{ii}}.{\hat{\kappa}})^{2}}\left[(m_{\textsc{ii}}.{\hat{\kappa}})\sin(u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}})-(n+m_{\textsc{ii}}.{\hat{\kappa}})\sin(u^{E}_{\textsc{ii}})\right]\bigg)\,,\end{split}

(8.4.11)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\delta_{n}P={}&\tfrac{1}{2}(n^{2}-1)\omega_{g}^{2}\sin^{2}(n\omega\Delta\ell)\\
&\times\bigg(\frac{\mathring{H}(\check{k}_{\textsc{i}},u,u^{R}_{\textsc{i}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,\check{k}_{\textsc{i}})}+\frac{\mathring{H}(k_{\textsc{i}},u^{R}_{\textsc{i}},u^{E}_{\textsc{i}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,k_{\textsc{i}})}+\frac{\mathring{H}(\check{k}_{\textsc{ii}},u,u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,\check{k}_{\textsc{ii}})}+\frac{\mathring{H}(k_{\textsc{ii}},u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}},u^{E}_{\textsc{ii}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,k_{\textsc{ii}})}\bigg)\,,\end{split}

(8.4.12)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\delta_{K}P={}&\tfrac{1}{2}n^{2}\omega_{g}\omega\sin^{2}(n\omega\Delta\ell)\\
&\times\bigg(\frac{h(m_{\textsc{i}},m_{\textsc{i}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,\check{k}_{\textsc{i}})}\bigg|^{u}_{u^{R}_{\textsc{i}}}+\frac{h(m_{\textsc{i}},m_{\textsc{i}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,k_{\textsc{i}})}\bigg|^{u^{R}_{\textsc{i}}}_{u^{E}_{\textsc{i}}}+\frac{h(m_{\textsc{ii}},m_{\textsc{ii}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,\check{k}_{\textsc{ii}})}\bigg|^{u}_{u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}}}+\frac{h(m_{\textsc{ii}},m_{\textsc{ii}})}{\gamma^{(0)}(\kappa,k_{\textsc{ii}})}\bigg|^{u^{R}_{\textsc{ii}}}_{u^{E}_{\textsc{ii}}}\bigg)\,.\end{split}

(8.4.13)

This confirms the results of
[
21
]
and generalises them beyond the vacuum case
n=1
: the terms
\delta_{\psi}P
,
\delta_{\mathscr{A}}P
and
\delta_{K}P
are trivial modifications of the corresponding expressions for vacuum, while the term
\delta_{n}P
has no counterpart in the vacuum case.

Notably, both in vacuum and in dielectrics, the perturbation of the polarisation vectors produce no (linear) perturbation of the output intensity. This is because
\epsilon
-perturbations of these vectors produce only
\epsilon^{2}
terms in their inner products with the unperturbed vectors.

As in
[
21
]
,
\delta_{\psi}P
can be attributed to the GW perturbation of the optical phase, and
\delta_{K}P
corresponds to a perturbation of the EM frequency, which rescales the unperturbed signal (as can be seen from the
\sin^{2}(\omega\Delta\ell)
term).
While in vacuum the perturbation of the amplitude produces only one correction similar to
\delta_{\mathscr{A}}P
, in the case of
n\neq 1
there is a further term
\delta_{n}P
arising from the difference in propagation speeds of the electromagnetic and gravitational waves.

8.5
Low Frequency Limit

For current interferometers, the arm lengths are short compared to the gravitational wavelength, so that it suffices to expand to leading order in
\omega_{g}\ell_{\textsc{i}}
and
\omega_{g}\ell_{\textsc{ii}}
.
Moreover, the difference in the arm lengths is typically very small:
\Delta\ell/\ell\ll 1
. Neglecting relative errors of this size, we replace
\ell_{\textsc{i}}
and
\ell_{\textsc{ii}}
by
\ell
everywhere except in the multiplicative factors
\sin^{2}(n\omega\Delta\ell)
and
\sin(n\omega\Delta\ell)
.
Using these approximations, we obtain

\displaystyle\delta_{\psi}P

\displaystyle\approx\tfrac{1}{2}n\omega\ell\sin(2n\omega\Delta\ell)[h(m_{\textsc{i}},m_{\textsc{i}})-h(m_{\textsc{ii}},m_{\textsc{ii}})]\,,

(8.5.1)

\displaystyle\delta_{\mathscr{A}}P

\displaystyle\approx-\tfrac{1}{2}n\omega_{g}\ell\sin^{2}(n\omega\Delta\ell)\left[h^{\prime}(m_{\textsc{i}},m_{\textsc{i}})\frac{1-({\hat{\kappa}}.m_{\textsc{i}})^{2}}{n^{2}-({\hat{\kappa}}.m_{\textsc{i}})^{2}}+h^{\prime}(m_{\textsc{ii}},m_{\textsc{ii}})\frac{1-({\hat{\kappa}}.m_{\textsc{ii}})^{2}}{n^{2}-({\hat{\kappa}}.m_{\textsc{ii}})^{2}}\right]\,,

(8.5.2)

\displaystyle\delta_{n}P

\displaystyle\approx-\tfrac{1}{2}n\omega_{g}\ell(n^{2}-1)\sin^{2}(n\omega\Delta\ell)\left[\frac{h^{\prime}(m_{\textsc{i}},m_{\textsc{i}})}{n^{2}-({\hat{\kappa}}.m_{\textsc{i}})^{2}}+\frac{h^{\prime}(m_{\textsc{ii}},m_{\textsc{ii}})}{n^{2}-({\hat{\kappa}}.m_{\textsc{ii}})^{2}}\right]\,,

(8.5.3)

\displaystyle\delta_{K}P

\displaystyle\approx n\omega_{g}\ell\sin^{2}(n\omega\Delta\ell)\left[h^{\prime}(m_{\textsc{i}},m_{\textsc{i}})+h^{\prime}(m_{\textsc{ii}},m_{\textsc{ii}})\right]\,,

(8.5.4)

where

h^{\prime}(m,m)=\partial_{u}h(m,m)=-A(m,m)\sin(u)\,.

(8.5.5)

In the low frequency limit, the perturbations “beyond the eikonal”,
\delta_{\mathscr{A}}P
,
\delta_{n}P
and
\delta_{K}P
, have a similar form and can thus be summarised as

\begin{split}\delta_{b\psi}P:=&\;\delta_{\mathscr{A}}P+\delta_{n}P+\delta_{K}P\\
\approx&\;\tfrac{1}{2}n\omega_{g}\ell\sin^{2}(\omega\Delta\ell)[h^{\prime}(m_{\textsc{i}},m_{\textsc{i}})+h^{\prime}(m_{\textsc{ii}},m_{\textsc{ii}})]\,,\end{split}

(8.5.6)

Factoring out trigonometric functions depending on the GW phase and the interferometer arm lengths, and splitting the GW polarisation into the two polarisation states as
A=\alpha_{+}A_{+}+\alpha_{\times}A_{\times}
, where
\alpha_{+}
and
\alpha_{\times}
denote the amplitudes of the respective polarisation modes, see
[
21
]
, the detector response in the low frequency limit takes the form

\displaystyle\delta_{\psi}P

\displaystyle=n\omega\ell\cos(u)\sin(2n\omega\Delta\ell)(\alpha_{+}F_{+}+\alpha_{\times}F_{\times})\,,

(8.5.7)

\displaystyle\delta_{b\psi}P

\displaystyle=n\omega_{g}\ell\sin(u)\sin(n\omega\Delta\ell)^{2}(\alpha_{+}f_{+}+\alpha_{\times}f_{\times})\,,

(8.5.8)

with the detector response pattern functions

\displaystyle F_{\lambda}

\displaystyle=+\tfrac{1}{2}[A_{\lambda}(m_{\textsc{i}},m_{\textsc{i}})-A_{\lambda}(m_{\textsc{ii}},m_{\textsc{ii}})]\,,

(8.5.9)

\displaystyle f_{\lambda}

\displaystyle=-\tfrac{1}{2}[A_{\lambda}(m_{\textsc{i}},m_{\textsc{i}})+A_{\lambda}(m_{\textsc{ii}},m_{\textsc{ii}})]\,,

(8.5.10)

where
\lambda
takes the values
+
and
\times
.
Parametrising the GW propagation direction and polarisation using Euler angles
\Phi,\Theta,\Psi
as in
[
21
]
with the polarisation angle
\Psi
set to zero as usual, we find

\displaystyle F_{+}

\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}(1+\cos^{2}\Theta)\cos 2\Phi\,,

\displaystyle F_{\times}

\displaystyle=-\cos\Theta\sin 2\Phi\,,

(8.5.11)

\displaystyle f_{+}

\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\sin^{2}\Theta\cos 2\Phi\,,

\displaystyle f_{\times}

\displaystyle=0\,,

(8.5.12)

as in
[
21
]
(which was concerned with vacuum only).
The function
f_{\times}
vanishes identically, and the remaining functions
F_{+}
,
F_{\times}
and
f_{+}
are plotted (in absolute values) in
Figure

2
.

(a)

Pattern function
F_{+}

(b)

Pattern function
F_{\times}

(c)

Pattern function
f_{+}

Figure 2
:
Detector response pattern functions for vacuum (
n=1
). The left two panels (a) and (b) show the normalised eikonal response, while the rightmost panel (c) shows the corrections beyond the eikonal.

In the low-frequency limit, the presence of a dielectric thus results merely in a rescaling of the detector response by the refractive index
n
, as can be seen from (
8.5.7
).

8.6
Comparison with Fibre Optics

Finally, we compare our results (applying to plane waves in infinitely extended dielectrics) with those of
[
20
]
for guided waves in step-index optical fibres.
As the final expressions given there are restricted to one-way propagation of light in the low frequency limit, we consider the same setting here.

For one-way light propagation, the phase perturbation in the current setup reads

\delta\psi=-\tfrac{1}{2}nA(m,m)\frac{\sin(u)-\sin(u+(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})\omega_{g}m.x)}{\Omega(n-m.{\hat{\kappa}})}

(8.6.1)

where
\Omega=\omega_{g}/\omega
and
u=\omega_{g}(\mathchoice{{\hat{\kappa}}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{{\hat{\kappa}}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{{\hat{\kappa}}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{{\hat{\kappa}}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}\mathchoice{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}-t)+\chi
, cf. (
6.1.60
).
Evaluating this at a distance
\ell
from the point of emission, at
\mathchoice{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{x^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\ell\mathchoice{m^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{m^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{m^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{m^{{{i}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
, the low-frequency limit
\omega_{g}\ell\ll 1
yields

\delta\psi=\tfrac{1}{2}nA(m,m)\cos(-\omega_{g}t+\chi)\omega\ell+O(\omega_{g}\ell)\,,

(8.6.2)

which is to be compared with the phase perturbation in optical fibres
[
20
, Eq. (6.11)]

\delta\psi_{\text{fibre}}=\tfrac{1}{2}c_{1}A(m,m)\cos(-\omega_{g}t+\chi)+O(\omega_{g}\ell)

(8.6.3)

(with the phase offset
\chi
added as needed), where we have adapted the overall sign of the phase for consistency with the sign convention used here.
The multiplicative coefficient
c_{1}
in (
8.6.3
)
had to be determined numerically as a function of the core and cladding refractive indices
n_{1}
,
n_{2}
, and also of the core radius
\rho
, but was generally found to be close to the effective refractive index
c_{1}\approx\bar{n}\approx n_{1}

[
20
, Sect. 8]
.
Hence, we find good agreement of the phase perturbations acquired by plane waves in infinitely extended dielectrics and Bessel modes of azimuthal mode index
m=1
in step-index optical fibres.

Concerning perturbations of the amplitude and polarisation, we note that such effects arise in the current setup only at next-to-leading order in the ratio
\omega_{g}/\omega
, which was neglected in
[
20
]
. Nonetheless, perturbations of this kind were obtained for optical fibres
[
20
, Sect. 7]
, but they were found to be suppressed relatively to the phase perturbation by a factor
(1-n_{2}/n_{1})^{2}
which vanishes in the case considered here.
So although the results for the amplitude and polarisation perturbations are not directly comparable, they agree to the extent that such effects in media are smaller than the phase perturbation by a factor of
\omega_{g}/\omega
.
In any case a more accurate comparison of such effects can only be obtained by repeating the calculations here using Bessel waves in lieu of plane waves.

9
Discussion

We have computed the perturbation of monochromatic plane wave solutions of Maxwell’s equations due to a plane gravitational wave and determined the
resulting signal in Michelson interferometers.

While the problem is simpler in the commonly used geometric optics approximation, the validity of such an approximation was not clear. Our analysis of the full Maxwell equations confirms its validity, putting the approximation on firm grounds. The unperturbed electromagnetic field, together with its first order perturbation, can indeed be approximated to current experimental accuracy by using a form which separates amplitude and phase, with the amplitude function analytic in the frequency ratio
\omega_{g}/\omega
within the setup considered here.

By computing both phase and amplitude perturbations for arbitrary incidence angles of the gravitational wave, our result generalises previous ones which have either allowed for arbitrary incidence angles but have neglected amplitude perturbations
[
19
]
or, conversely, described amplitude or polarisation perturbations only for specific alignments
[
18
,
14
,
26
]
.

Moreover, by including a dielectric refractive index, we were able to generalise our previous result
[
21
]
(which relied on the geometric optics approximation), and compare with analogous calculations for fibre optics
[
20
]
. In both cases, we find agreement of the essential results.

While we admit that the calculations presented here are unlikely to have a direct impact on signal analysis and interpretation of current gravitational wave detectors, we stress that previous models based on geometric optics relied on the tacit assumption that the true solution of the Maxwell equations in this setup admits a convergent eikonal expansion. Our analysis here describes a model where this is indeed the case.

(A.12)

In all terms involving derivatives of the metric (i.e. its time derivative, Christoffel symbols or the Ricci tensor), we may use the unperturbed expression for the electromagnetic field.

(D.5)

so that the energy density is seen to be given by

(D.6)

Appendix E
Compatibility of Reflection with Constraints

Consider the reflection conditions

\displaystyle\nu\cdot(\check{Z}-Z^{*})

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle\nu\times(\check{Z}+Z^{*})

\displaystyle=0\,,

(E.1)

where
Z
is the incident field,
\check{Z}
is the reflected field, and
\nu
is the normal to the reflecting surface.
This can be covariantly rewritten using the complex tensor
\mathcal{F}
defined in (
B.5
):

\mathchoice{(\check{\mathcal{F}}-\mathcal{F}^{*})^{{{\alpha}{\beta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{(\check{\mathcal{F}}-\mathcal{F}^{*})^{{{\alpha}{\beta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{(\check{\mathcal{F}}-\mathcal{F}^{*})^{{{\alpha}{\beta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{(\check{\mathcal{F}}-\mathcal{F}^{*})^{{{\alpha}{\beta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\nu_{\beta}=0\,.

(E.2)

Let us verify that this prescription is consistent in the following sense: if the incident field
Z
satisfies the constraint equation which arises from Maxwell’s equations, then so does the reflected field
\check{Z}
.
Recall that the constraint equation is obtained from the time-evolution equation by contraction with the conormal
\nu_{i}
. Note that since
\nu_{i}
is proportional to
m_{i}
, we may use the latter instead, which has the advantage that all its derivatives vanish.
By assumption, the incident field
Z
satisfies the (conjugate) constraint equation

n\partial_{0}(m_{i}Z^{*i})-j\varepsilon^{ijk}\partial_{j}(m_{i}Z^{*}_{k})=0\,.

(E.3)

Using
m_{i}Z^{*i}=m_{i}\check{Z}^{i}
and
\varepsilon^{ijk}m_{i}Z^{*}_{k}=-\varepsilon^{ijk}m_{i}\check{Z}_{k}
, we obtain

n\partial_{0}(m_{i}\check{Z}^{i})+j\varepsilon^{ijk}\partial_{j}(m_{i}\check{Z}_{k})=0\,,

(E.4)

so the reflected field indeed satisfies the constraint equation. The remaining projections of Maxwell’s equations then determine the normal derivatives of the various components of
Z
, thereby encoding the law of reflection.

In fact, we can formulate a covariant argument which shows that the requirement that partial derivatives of
m
vanish is inessential. Since
\nu
is hypersurface-orthogonal, it can be locally written as
\nu=g\,\mathrm{d}f
, where
f
and
g
are smooth functions. By linearity, we may equally formulate the reflection condition with the exact form
df
instead of
\nu
:

\mathchoice{\check{\mathcal{F}}^{{{\alpha}{\beta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\check{\mathcal{F}}^{{{\alpha}{\beta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\check{\mathcal{F}}^{{{\alpha}{\beta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\check{\mathcal{F}}^{{{\alpha}{\beta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{f^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.2639pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.2639pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.36111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.97221pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{;}{\beta}}}}{f^{{\mathcho (E.6)

Since the connection used is torsion-free,
\mathchoice{f^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.2639pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.2639pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.36111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.97221pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{;}{\beta}{\alpha}}}}{f^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.2639pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.2639pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.36111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.97221pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{;}{\beta}{\alpha}}}}{f^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.2639pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.2639pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.36111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.97221pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{;}{\beta}{\alpha}}}}{f^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.2639pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.2639pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.36111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.97221pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox is symmetric, so the last term vanishes due to the anti-symmetry of the field tensors.
Thus,

satisfies the constraint equation
